speechtext: Hon. Sir WILLIAM MULOCK (Postmaster General) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 162) to consolidate and amend the Acts respecting Alien Labour.
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to explain ?

Mr. Speaker, although the Bill is entitled ' an Act to' amend, consolidate and amend the Acts respecting Alien Labour,' it will be necessary to amend that title inasmuch as it is not a consolidation. The provisions of the present Bill are as follows : ,
One section of the Bill amends section 1 of the Alien Labour Act, 1897. That original section provides that it is an offence to import alien labour under contract. It was found that this provision could be easily evaded by the contract not being made abroad, and therefore it is proposed to strengthen the clause by making it a;n offence to import under a promise or offer of employment.
Another section containing a number ot subsections provides machinery whereby employers may obtain judicial permission to import labour that cannot be procured in Canada. At present the spirit of the Act, so far as it is enforcible, is stringent, and it is represented that in many cases labour not procurable in Canada could not be lawfully imported. It is expedient that under these circumstances a measure should be adopted to meet such a situation so that there would be no inducement to persons in need of labour of a particular class to import illegally that class of labour. The machinery provided by this Bill contemplates an application to a judge for permission. That application will require to be published in the press and a hearing of the application can be conducted in the open court as in civil causes. All parties interested have a right to appear and if the judge is

of opinion that the application should be granted, he may do so, setting forth the extent to which he grants the leave and to the extent to which he grants the leave the order is an authority to the employer to import the persons authorized by the order.
Another section amends section 3 of the Act of 1897, which was further amended by the statutes of 1901. That section as it stands to-day requires the consent of a certain functionary to the bringing of an action for a violation of the provisions of the Alien Labour Act. The proposed section dispenses with any such preliminary sanction.
Under the law as it is to-day it is declared illegal to induce people to come into Canada in contravention of the Act by promise of employment by advertisements. It has been held by a judge of the Supreme Court in the province of British Columbia that an advertisement, for example, such as ' wanted,' naming a large number of men, and other inducements which might be or might not be correct, was not an offence against the law inasmuch as the advertisement could not be held to he a promise. It is proposed therefore to add to this section after the word ' employment,'
-or by representations justifying reasonable expectation of employment.
There are some other verbal changes.
Another section deals with the case of inducing people to come to Canada by false representations. This spring there was an illustration of the injury done by men inducing people to come to Canada by false representations. It appears that a very large number of Italians, going up to the thousands, reached Montreal this spring in search for employment under circumstances that amounted to a serious fraud upon these people, and a demoralization of the labour market of Montreal and perhaps of other portions of Canada. A commission was issued to inquire into the circumstances attending the bringing in of those men. The commissioner has not yet reported, but his investigation was conducted in open court, and the press reported somewhat fully the evidence given. I do not purpose at this moment to state in any detail the nature of the evidence, but I think that any one wno has perused so much of it as appeared in the press cannot but reach the conclusion that the methods adopted to induce these unfortunate people to come to Canada were criminal and cruel in the extreme. They were brought into Canada by the most grossly false representations originating in Montreal, by a scheme of fraud for the enrichment of men in Montreal to bring men here thousands of miles from their own homes, and, when they reached Montreal, to induce them to contribute money to the persons promoting this agency, in the deluded belief that they would thereby immediately secure profitable employment. The scheme seemed to be conceived and carried out in Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
fraud. It is proposed by this section to make such false representations as to the state of the labour market a criminal offence.
Another section proposes to incorporate into law the spirit of the clauses introduced into the Crow's Nest Pass Railway Contract, requiring the work on lines constructed by a railway subsidized or aided by the government either by gift or loan of money or guarantee or other valuable consideration to be carried on in accordance with the spirit of the clauses made applicable to that contract. Hon. gentleman are familiar with the provisions of that contract. They are to the effect that, wherever possible, the labour shall be British or Canadian labour, and that in case contracts are made with companies for the work of construction, the companies shall be incorprated in Canada under Dominion or provincial legislation, the majority of the directors shall be citizens of this empire and the majority of the capital shall be owned by citizens of the empire.
Another section provides that persons infringing the Act by importing the classes of labour in question, that is in violation of the law, shall be liable for the expense of their deportation to the country from which they came, and obligations are also cast upon the ships bringing out persons of this class knowing, or having reasonable ground for believing, that they have been brought here in contravention of the law. Then some other provisions of the Bill deal with undesirable classes of people, not being brought here in connection with labour at all, and it is proposed to prohibit from landing or remaining in Canada any of the following classes :
Idiots, insane persons, paupers, or persons likely to become a public charge, professional beggars, persons afflicted with loathsome or dangerous contagious diseases, polygamists, anarchists or persons who believe in or advocate the overthrow by force or violence of all forms of law, the constituted authority of the country or the assassination of public officials, prostitutes, and persons who procure or attempt to bring in prostitutes or women for the purpose of prostitution ; persons who have been within one year deported or ordered to be deported from Canada for having entered Canada in violation of any of the provisions of the said Act of 1897 as amended, or of this Act, and of persons convicted of a crime involving moral turpitude; provided that this shall not be held to exclude from Canada persons convicted of offences purely political, not involving moral turpitude.
Another section deals with the liability of the owners of and persons interested in the vessel that aids in any violation of this Act. Another section provides for the arrest of any alien brought in in contravention of the law, and for his detention while waiting to be transferred to the vessel to be sent back to his own country. Another section gives the Minister of Labour, instead of as

at present Attorney General, the authority for ordering deportation. Another section authorizes the Governor in Council to appoint special officers for the enforcement of the law and to pass necessary regulations for its more effective working. Another section provides that in case His Majestj should be obliged to defray any expenses in the first place connected with the deportation of persons illegally brought into the country there shall be a clause of action over by the Crown against the persons primarily the cause of such prohibited labour or persons having entered Canada. There are some provisions that I have not alluded to, but they will more fully appear when the Bill is printed and placed in the hands of lion, gentlemen.	,

I would ask the hon. Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) if there is any provision in the Bill to oblige them to inspect immigrants before they are allowed to leave the port from which the ship sails, because, unless that is a part of the law, I think it would be very deficient. We saw a case of that kind when the steamer ' Lake Simcoe ' landed a number of Syrians the other day. It appeared to me that had there been an efficient inspection at Havre, France, the ship would not have taken any of them on board. The owners of the ship have had to become responsible for twenty-nine that were allowed to come over without any visible meant of support. More than thirty of them have had to be deported and there are a large number of others who are subject to treatment. That is an important provision and should be enacted in the Bill.

There is much in the remark of my hon. friend (Mr. Wilson), but perhaps when he has looked at the Bill he will find that clause 14, or at all events one of the clauses near the end of the Bill, authorizes the Governor in Council to appoint special officers in order to accomplish the object of the Bill. If the object of the Bill, for instance, is to exclude from landing in Canada any undesirable classes of persons, my hon. friend's proposal would be in harmony with the clause that the Governor in Council should appoint such officers as are necessary in order to give effect to that prohibitory clause. It would strike me as a very wise thing that these proscribed classes should be intercepted at the earliest moment. If the government is of the opinion that it would be wise to have such examination made before the vessel sails I think my hon. friend will find that the measure proposes to give the government full authority to make any such arrangement.

I, of course, do not propose to discuss the Bill at this stage. May I ask whether or not the Bill 251
has been printed or is it introduced with the intention of having it printed? Has the printing been expedited in any way ?
It is not sufficiently printed to enable me to hand my hon. friend a copy, but it was printed in galley form and has been revised.
What I desire to suggest is that the printing may be expedited as much as possible. It is, we hope, a very late hour in the session and we would like to see it as soon as possible.
I will try to have it in galley form in the hands of my hon. friends to-morrow morning. I will send a number of copies so that other hon. gentlemen may be able to see it.

Is it the intention to have the evidence which is being taken by Judge Winchester respecting employment of aliens on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and respecting the influx of Italian labour into the city of Montreal printed and distributed for the use of members of the House ?

It is intended to have it printed at the earliest possible moment, but it will not be possible to have it printed before prorogation if it takes place at an early date. As soon as the inquiry is completed I will have it printed and distributed. The inquiry has not yet been completed, but I was informed by Judge Winchester, who passed through Ottawa on his way from Montreal a few days ago, that there only remained the examination of Mr. Lumsden and perhaps the cross-examination of Sir Sandford Fleming as he has not been able yet to conclude the evidence of these two gentlemen.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called it is my sad duty to have to inform the House that we have lost anbther of our colleagues in the person of Mr. Isidore Proulx. member for the electoral district of Prescott. As is well known by most members of the House Mr. Proulx had been in poor health for many months past. He had undergone last autumn an operation which he bore with great fortitude, and it was hoped that it had checked the disease, but unfortunately the vital forces were gone and he was carried away at a comparatively early period. He left us last week with the intention of coming back but we are not to see lum any more in this House. Mr. Proulx was a quiet, unobtrusive member of this House, but very much respected by all of those who came in contact with him. and I can bear testimony that he was as



faithful a friend as ever lived. I am sure that hon. members on both sides of the House will join in sympathizing with the bereaved family in the sad mourning through which they are now passing.

I desire to join in the expression to which the Prime Minister has given utterance with regard to Mr. Proulx. While it is true that I did not enjoy an intimate acquaintance with him, nevertheless I learned to know him sufficiently to respect and appreciate him. I am sure that ail of us on this side of the House will join in the sympathy and condolence Which the Prime Minister on this occasion has so fittingly expressed.
Before you proceed with government orders, there is a matter to which I wish to draw attention. I sent for the Minister of Militia

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend is going to make a personal explanation, I might state that the House will be moved into supply in a few minutes, and he will have a better opportunity then of disclosing his grievance.
I have no personal explanation to make. It is a matter in connection with an article in the paper this morning, and I think this is the proper time to bring it up ; is it not ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think not. It would be more opportune to do so when the House is moved into supply.

It will not take more than a moment. In the ' Citizen ' this morning, under the heading
Attempt to Dragoon-Methods of the Martinet to Stifle Criticism-Minister of Militia Takes Revenge Upon the Canadian Military Gazette for Daring to Disapprove of His Course in Dundonald Exposures.
I find an article referring to a letter signed by L. J. Pinault, Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, addressed to the proprietors of the * Canadian Military Gazette.' The letter is dated 28th of June, and reads :
Department of Militia and Defence,
Ottawa, June 28. 1904.
Sir,-I am directed by the Honourable the Minister of Militia and Defence to inform you that the agreement entered into with the Canadian Military Gazette, by my letter of the 29th August, 1903, will terminate on the 30th September next, from which date this department will not hold itself responsible for the publication and payment thereof of the Royal Military College advertisement and the Militia General Orders.
I have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant,
(Signed)	L. J. PINAULT,
Colonel,
Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence.
The proprietors of the Canadian Military Gazette.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The paper says :
It seems superfluous to comment on this letter. It tells the publishers of the * Gazette ' very plainly that the minister does not approve of its recent policy in the Dundonald exposures and gives it until September 30 to make amends. If it does not do so a considerable part of its revenue will be cut off.
This is the third time this payment has been withdrawn in an effort to influence the ' Gazette.' The threat will have no more influence now than on the two former occasions. The * Gazette ' will continue to pursue the policy that all honest men believe to be in the best interests of the country-for the militia and country are one.
In an editorial comment the ' Citizen ' very properly points out:
The idea that men who volunteer their services to the country in most instances for nothing or at a sacrifice of both time and money, should also be expected to surrender their liberty as citizens not only when on duty but when in civilian life is too ridiculous for consideration, unless the object is to ruin the militia force of this country entirely. The members of the militia make enough sacrifices as it is out of patriotism to keep up a force that should be kept up by the country in such a manner as to at least make the sacrifice part of it unnecessary.
Then follows an illustration of the power of the minister, or of a general, or of any officer to control any officer or man under him, when he is not on duty or in uniform, and it illustrates the case of Sir Mackenzie Bowel! when years ago he was major in the militia, and when the general officer commanding sought to influence him and dragoon him for certain expressions to which he had given utterance. In view of the great importance of this question to civil liberty, and in view of the erroneous impression that the officers of the force all over the country have, I think it is proper that some attention should be paid to the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry the hon. gentleman did not take my suggestion. He is out of order altogether, and the only way he can put himself in order is to move the adjournment of the House.

Well, I can move the adjournment of the House. Section 72 of the proposed Militia Act reads :
72. The Army Act for the time being in force in the United Kingdom, the King's Regulations, and all other laws applicable to His Majesty's troops in Canada and not inconsistent with this Act or the regulations made thereunder, shall have force and effect as if they had been enacted by the parliament of Canada for the government of the militia, and every officer this Act or the regulations made thereunder, to from the time of being called out for active service, and also during the period of annual drill or training under the provisions of this Act, and also at any other time while upon military duty or in the uniform of his corps upon or within any rifle range or any armoury, or other place where arms, guns, ammunition or other military stores are kept, or any drill

shed or other building or place used for militia purposes, or during any drill or parade of his corps at which he is present in the ranks, when going to or from the place of drill or parade, and also whether in uniform or not at any drill or parade of his corps at which he is present as a spectator.
Subsection 2 :
2. Officers and men of the permanent force and members of the permanent staff of the militia shall at all times be subject to military law.
It is clear this last section applies only to the permanent force, which, of course, is subject to the military law throughout the year, but the militia force is not subject to military law except they are on duty or in the uniform of their corps. In order to encourage the officers and men of the permanent force to be free men, and to take an interest in military matters and let the public have the benefit of their views from time to time, I have given the minister notice that I intend to move the following amendment to section 79 of the Militia Bill :
Nothing in this Act shall at any time prevent any officer or man of the militia, except when on parade or on duty, from temperately expressing his views on questions affecting the welfare of the militia force and communicating suggestions, criticisms and statements thereon to the public of Canada.
If the hon. gentleman is going to discuss the Militia Bill, that is clearly out of order.
I am discussing civil liberty.
Humbug.

I find in the Toronto ' News ' of yesterday interviews from three prominent military men, which show that the military officers of the country do not understand that the men under them are absolutely free. I regret that a couple of these officers think they have power over their men when not on duty. For example, suppose a private in Col. Pellatt's regiment should assault him on the public street when not on duty or not in uniform, according to the generally expressed notion the colonel would have control of that soldier under the military law. That is not so. All the redress he could possibly have against him would be under the common law, under which he could be fined. I ask any one of these gentlemen, from the minister down, to point out where directly or indirectly the King's regulations or the Army Act authorizes the bringing of that man under the military law. We want to resist these attempts at dragooning ; we want to resist these attempts at establishing militarism in Canada. We have seen instances of Straffords, Lauds and Jeffreys and Robes-pierres, and democrats up to the hilt, becoming aristocrats, but there is only one way to preserve civil and religious liberty, 2511
and that is to check militarism and tyranny whether it is found in the Prime Minister or in his subordinate the Minister of Militia.
We want no dragooning in this country ; we want no muzzling of the public press or of private individuals in the Dominion of Canada. I move the adjournment of the House.

As to the letter which has been read, which appears to have been sent by the deputy minister of my department to the printing or publishing office, I can only say that I never saw the letter. I presume it is a business letter written to give notice at the beginning of the financial year, so that if it is thought desirable to terminate the contract, for which it is necessary to give three months' notice, that contract can be terminated. As to the military law, I cannot understand the hon. gentleman bringing the matter up now, seeing that, as he says himself, he has given notice that when the Bill comes up for ' third reading he is going to propose an amendment. I shall be prepared, when that time arrives, to discuss it. I cannot understand why he attempts to precipitate a discussion upon it at this moment.

Mr. Speaker, I think it would be well if some of our militia colonels went on a pilgrimage with the Doukho-bors, or engaged in a struggle with the spirit wrestlers, and gave the sane people of this country a little time to attend to the ordinary affairs of life.
I want to draw attention to the exact wording of the letter : ' I am directed by the Minister of Militia and Defence to inform you.'
What is the date ot the letter ?
The date is June 28, 1904. Surely these words are specific enough.
Every letter sent out from my department is couched in similar phraseology. I am responsible, of course.
Might I ask the minister at what period the fiscal year ends-the 30th of September or when ?
The 30th of June.
The advertisement, I understand, runs to the 30th of September.
Three months' notice is required to have a contract for any advertisement terminated.
Can the minister recollect if similar notices were sent to other journals publishing this notice of the military school?

There is no other journal publishing that advertisement.

In all other journals the advertisement is inserted for one issue in the year only.
Has it been the practice to send a letter like this to this journal at the close of each previous fiscal year ?

I am not aware, hut I think so. I cannot speak positively.
Motion (Mr. Sam. Hughes) to adjourn, negatived.
['Since my hon. friend (Mr. Galliher) agrees, I move that the debate be now adjourned.']
FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair I have a resolution to propose, and I wish to make a few remarks with regard to it. The resolution, I may say at the outset, is one censuring the government for not taking that care with regard to the transportation of perishable products from the point of origin to the markets of the world that I think they ought to have taken, and that the opportunities which have presented themselves from time to time enabled them to do. The perishable products of the country are among the most valuable of our exports, not only in the aggregate, but intrinsically. Our total exports of agricultural products for the year ending the 30th of June, 1903, amounted to $114,441,863, of which nearly one-half, or $52,880,153 were perishable products, which require special care in their transportation to the markets of the world to enable the pioducers to get full value for them, therefore seems to me particularly incumbent upon the government of the day to look carefully after this matter. These products are the most valuable of our exports. On account of the skill required to Produce them, they generally yield more profit than those articles in which there is a great deal of competition. Consequently the production of these perishable articles ought to be encouraged in this country. The chief item among these exports is cheese, of which we export close upon $25,000,000. Another is bacon and hams, of which we export close upon $16,000,000. These two articles require not cold storage, but simply a thoroughly ventilated storage for their transportation, not only on land in the cars, but in ships on the sea. They simply require the temperature of the outside air, which can be obtained by thorough ventilation. The next item on the list is butter, of which we exported in the year ending the 30th of .Tune, 1903, close on $7,000,000. This requires cold storage at a certain temperature over which the government should have control. The next item is fruit, of which we exported in the same vear $3,751,000. Some of it requires cold storage, but the greater portion Sir F. W. BORDEN.
requires only ventilated storage on shipboard ; and this can be got without any extra cost of freight and without any appreciable extra expense to the steamship owners.. It only requires the government to exercise that supervision and control that will enable the shipper to know positively that his products will have the temperature of the ocean air in crossing the ocean, in which case they will be landed in the old country markets in a sound condition to receive the highest prevailing prices. Any loss from lack of proper transportation facilities ultimately comes out of the pockets of the producer. To the extent to which the service is imperfect, to that extent the value of the product is depreciated. The depreciation from this cause in the value of the products shipped from Montreal amounts to many hundreds of thousands of dollars.
It may be said that our cold storage facilities are better than they once were. That is very true. We are certainly progressing. It would be strange if a government, in an enterprising country like Canada, were not able to imm'ove our facilities from year to year. It would indeed be strange if the transportation companies themselves did not greatly improve their facilities without any suggestion from the government at all. Formally years before we initiated cold storage we had the example of other British colonies which transported their perishable products across the tropics from the farthest corners of the world safely in cold storage, while we, who live only two weeks* journey from the British market, even yet. with all that experience of twenty years behind us, aie unable to ship these perishable products in a cold storage that is anything near perfection.
Last year the government had thermograph records taken of 155 cold storage chambers carrving these perishable products. In his report of 1902. the lion. Minister of Agriculture said that butter should be carried at a temperature of 20 degrees, and he stated afterwards that to bring about the best results you should have the chamber at 10 degrees.' But in these 155 records taken last year there is not one chamber that carried butter at a temperature of 10 degrees, and there are only 40 that touched a temperature of 20 degrees, and that was not the average across the ocean. Only 40 out of the 155 touched 20 degrees, and there was a very large number that carried the goods even above the freezing point. I would just enumerate a few of those. The Iona, of the Thompson line, which sailed July -o, 3903, carried butter, and the butter was put in at a temperature less than 40 degrees. The Minister of Agriculture seems to be always hunting for some excuse to explain why the steamers do not carry goods at the proper temperature, and he sometimes has for excuse the plea that the butter is put in hot. But in only two of these records does it appear that the butter was put in hot. In

this case the butter was put in at a temperature below 40, or 10 degrees lower than the temperature of the car in transit usually. Yet it never ran a point lower than 32, and that only when it arrives on the other side. On the ' Monteagle,' which sailed May 29, 1903, butter went in at a temperature of 40 degrees and never reached a point lower than 34, and that only on its arrival on the other side. On the ' Montford,' which sailed August 22nd, the butter was put in at a temperature a little higher, 45 degrees, and the temperature rapidly went down to 40, showing that the butter was not hot, but it never reached a temperature lower than 32 degrees at any point, and when it reached the other side it was 33 degrees. On the ' Montcalm ' the butter was put in at Montreal at 36 degrees, an exceedingly low temperature for butter to.be put in the chamber, but it never got lower than 34, and several days of the journey it was 156 or 37, or warmer than when put in. On the ' Montford,' which sailed September 27th, butter was put in at 38 degrees and never got lower than 36 at any time during the journey and a large portion of it was at 39. ' On the ' Corinthian,' which sailed October 8th, the butter was put in at 38, a very low temperature for butter to come out of the car, and never reached a point lower than 32, and that only after the expiration of ten days. On the 'Hungarian' the butter was put'in at tiie low temperature of 34 and never got below 31, and that in the early portion of the voyage. It gradually rose and came out at the other side at a temperature of 34.
Does the hon. gentleman mean that by the time of arrival, the time of arrival in the ship or at the shop where the butter is sold ?
What was the month ?

That steamer sailed August 22nd. On the ' Iona,' which sailed 5th of September from Montreal, the butter went in at a temperature of 66, but never got to a point at any time during the journey lower than 44. In other words, it took the whole of the journey across the ocean in cold storage chambers to bring the temperature down to 44, whereas a good cold'storage chamber would bring down the temperature in forty-eight or, at most, 72 hours, no matter how hot were the goods when put in, to a temperature as low as required. Then on the steamer ' Ionian,' which sailed from Montreal June 20th, the butter went in at 40 and never got below 38 during the whole journey. On the ' Kensington,' which sailed the 20th of June, the butter went in at 45, and only at the time of its arrival on the other side reached 30, or an average of about 36. On the ' Tunisian ' the butter went in at: 37 and never got bellow 35 dur ing the whole journey. On the ' Pretorian,' sailing July 11, the butter went in at 40 and never got below 35. On the ' Bavarian ' the butter went in at 34 and rose gradually to 35, and came out on the other side at 36. In other words, it was in better condition when it went on board than at any time during the journey, in so far as temperature was concerned. On the ' Pretorian,' which sailed 15th of August, the butter went in at 60, and the lowest point reached during the journey was 37. The temperature fluctuated from time to time 4 or 5 degrees every day, showing that the storage apparatus was not in proper order.
Then, the ' Canada,' sailing on 22nd August ; the butter went in at 54, and the lowest point touched during the voyage was 37, coming out, apparently, at the other side at 70. Whether that is a mistake or not, I do not know. I cannot imagine that such a thing would occur except by an accident. The butter in that case must have been very badly damaged. The lowest point reached was 37, or twenty-seven degrees higher than the minister himself and the experts say should be constantly maintained. The ' Pretorian,' sailing on September 19th, took in the butter at 55 ; lowest point reached 38, coming out on the other side at 40. The ' Lakonia,' sailing September 3rd : the butter went in at 50, and at no time in the voyage did the temperature go lower than 43. That

butter must have been almost ruined. It might as well have gone across in the ordinary storage, thus saving fifteen shillings a ton. Going in the ordinary ventilated storage it would have received just about as good treatment, so far as temperature is concerned, as in these cold storage chambers. In another chamber of the ' Lakonia ' the butter went in at 40, the lowest point reached was 37i, coming out on the other side at 38. The * Marina '; butter went in at 50, and the lowest point reached was 36, then rose to 40 and remained at about 40, coming out at that temperature at the other side. In another chamber of the ' Lakonia,' the butter went in at 50, reached 32 at the other side, the average temperature for the voyage being about 40. On the ' Kastalia,' the butter went in at 42, but rose immediately to 46, The temperature gradually went down and reached 34, or 24 degrees higher for the lowest point of the journey than the temperature which ought to be maintained according to the minister himself. On the ' Montcalm ' the butter went in at 44 and reached the other side at 32.
Now, I have taken up the time of the House in reading a large number of records in order to show that, out of 155 records taken there were something like 35 or 40 where the temperature never reached a point lower than the feezing, whereas, according to the minister himself a temperature of not more than 20 is necessary, and he and the experts now unite in saying that for good results the butter should toe carried at not higher than 10. I am sure everybody must agree with me that this is not a satisfactory condition of affairs. After an experience of carrying butter in cold storage by the different British colonies of twenty years and after an experience of this government of about nine years we still find that we are unable to carry a single shipment at the temperature which the experts tell us is required. Only about forty shipments ever reach that temperature during the whole journey, while about one-quarter of all the shipments were carried at a temperature above freezing point and many of them reached such a temperature that the butter must have been ruined in the voyage.
Now, who is to blame ? I contend that the government are entirely to blame. Ibis parliament voted willingly the large sum of money it thought necessary in order to secure this cold storage service Something like $150,000 was spent by this parliament in order to secure a good cold storage system. Half of the expense of putting in the cold storage chambers has been borne by the country. As against this. I wish to point out, the ships going to the ports of the United States pay for their own cold storage chambers ; the government of the United States does not go Mr. E. D. SMITH.
down into the pockets of the people to provide this outfit for the steamships. We have taken the people's money to pay for these improvements, in the hope that we would get a good service, and not only that, but in the hope of being able to control it. And, not only have we not got the service but we have absolutely no control. Not only have we spent the people's money to pay half the expense of providing this accommodation on the steamships, but we have given some of these lines at least enormous subsidies. The subsidy to the Allan Line was ostensibly to carry the mails; in reality it was to induce them to come to the ports of Montreal, Halifax and St. John regularly. Incidentally, in the last contract with the Allans, it was mentioned that they must provide cold storage chambers, We pay them a subsidy, besides paying half the expense of the cold storage chambers, and yet we have not an atom of control. They may carry the goods at any temperature they like. No government officer can step aboard and say :	You must carry these
goods at such and such a temperature. When the officers of the government go aboard these vessels they must go by the grace and favour of the company, and not by authority of this parliament or by any authority delegated to the ofiieers by this parliament.
Now, what ought the government to have done ? There are many courses they might have pursued. SMITH No power to inspect, and absolutely no control over the temperature, which is the one essential thing. But, even failing this the government had still another recourse. We have on our statute-books a law providing that no steamship shall sail from our ports carrying cattle until the government inspector has been aboard to see that proper provision is made for carrying the cattle-that certain space is allowed to each beast, that there is a certain width of alley-way, certain provisions for feeding, and so on. Why could not the government have a similar statute passed with regard to the cold storage and ventilated storage on vessels sailing from our ports and thus provide in a practical way for the carrying of these products of this vast industry representing not less than $52,000,000 a year ? But they neglected this third opportunity as they neglected every other. So, I am sure that anybody who studies the question will agree with me that the government are to blame that the shippers of this country have not proper cold storage facilities.
Now, the main portion of these perishable products, cheese, apples and meats, are carried in the ordinary stowage, not in cold storage. This is the most important matter of all. It is very important that we should have the six or seven millions worth of butter which we export, carried in cold storage and some of the fruit ; but we still have thirty-five millions worth of goods ter which we export, carried in cold storage, simply the pure air of the ocean which costs practically nothing. It has been
pointed out time and time again that all that was necessary was to provide that exhaust fans should be put on the steamers, which could be done at a trifling cost, and the ocean air sent through the holds of these vessels. If that were done all these exports could be landed on the other side in perfect condition and we could get full value instead of having a depreciation of millions of dollars every year on our apple crop. Prof. Robertson said before a committee of this House, that we would lose three millions dollars on the cheese export, which was verified the next year. All this enormous loss takes place simply because the ocean vessels and the cars in which the goods are taken from the point of origin to the sea-board are not ventilated. It has been pointed out that this can be done easily and cheaply, but all that the minister has ever done has been to send circular letters to the steamship companies, asking them to do it, asking them, out of the goodness of their hearts, to provide this facility. He has taken no power to control them that would enable the government to compel the companies to install this ventilation which would enable these products to be carried in good condition. He took no power to do this, but in his wisdom he thought he would provide something better, so he came to this House and asked for large sums of money to provide for what he calls a cool air service. This parliament voted willingly something over $100,000 to provide a cool air service, which is a sort of hybrid between cold storage and ventilated storage. What is the result ? Last year of a total export of 229,000,000 pounds of cheese, 3,000,000 pounds were carried in the cool air and 22G,000,000 pounds in ordinary stowage. Out of 2,000,000 barrels of apples, only 8,000 barrels were carried in the refrigerated air. Why ? Not because it is not a good thing, for the cool air is all right and it would be a good thing to carry these products all in cool air storage or better still in cold storage, but there is a charge of ten shillings a ton on butter and cheese and Is. 6d. a barrel on every barrel of apples placed in the cool air, although the minister stated that there .(Would be no extra charge for the cool air carriage. of Is. 6d. per barrel on apples and 10 shillings a ton on butter and cheese. All shippers and all experts agree that the only practicable way in which you can get ocean air through the holds of these vessels is by an exhaust fan or forced draft. I find on looking over the records that there was only a limited number of steamers that were provided with exhaust fans, that there was a great number that had no ventilation whatever and that many of them only had the trunk ventilation. That is simply an opening that will allow steam to get out but which is of no use whatever for the purpose of ventilation. Others had what is known as the cowl ventilation. That system is very good if the wind is not blowing in the same direction as that in which the steamer is going, because then the air is carried down to the bottom of the cargo, passes up through it and out, but if the wind is blowing in the same direction as the steamer is going the cowl system is no good at all. The cowl system, however, is a great deal better than having no ventilation at all provided the air is driven to the bottom of the cargo and there is an opening at the top of the chamber that will enable the air 'to get out. It is forced out by the impact of the air against the cowl ventilator. The air is taken to the bottom of the cargo, it is then forced up and comes out at the top of the chamber. A considerable number of vessels are fitted with these cowl ventilators, but all should be fitted with exhaust fans. If the vessels that were fitted with these fans had them in operation all the time and if they had them in every chamber, that would be what we want, but I am awarb that a great many of the chambers are not fitted with these fans at all. The report simply states that there are exhaust fans on certain steamers, but I find on. some of these steamers that whereas there is an exhaust fan in one chamber there is no ventilation in another chamber, so that we do not know what the system of ventilation is upon any steamer. As a matter of fact there are a number of these steamers that have not even the cowl system of ventilation.	For instance, the ' Lake Champlain ' has only intakes, the ' Ontarian ' has only fans in one

The right hon. minister has admitted that the ventilation of the holds of vessels carrying perishable cargo is of enormous benefit, but instead of taking advantage of the opportunities, instead of seeing that remedies are provided, the government have done nothing effective in regard to it. I want to show by a few of the thermograph records that the temperature in the holds of these vessels where there are supposed to be fans is not what it ought to be. These twelve returns brought down, although there is no opportunity of comparing them with the records of a thermograph placed on deck giving the proper temperature of the ocean air, show that even though there are fans on the vessels they are not operated as they are supposed to be and that there is really no ventilation. On the 22nd of August the ' Canada ' sailed out of the port of Montreal. The temperature commenced at 60 degrees, it goes down to 55, for a large portion of the journey it remains at 55, and on the other side it goes up to 67, at no time reaching higher than 67. There is ample evidence that this steamer was ventilated at any rate during a large portion of the voyage. The temperature recorded is about the temperature of the ocean air. It is also about the temperature of the cool air chambers provided by the government at an expense of $100,000. For instance, take the ' Cervona ' fitted with cool air chambers for the use of which a large additional charge is made. The goods went in at a temperature of 68 degrees and at no time did the temperature reach a lower point than; 54 degrees. Thajt is almost identical with the temperature in ordinary ventilated stowage, where the exhaust fans are in operation,, or where by some system the cool air of the ocean is introduced and forced through the cargo. For a large portion of the journey the temperature was 55 degrees in ordinary ventilated storage, just one degree higher than in the ' cool air ' chambers. This simply bears out what I have contended time and again, and it is that the temperature of the ocean, if we can get it through the cargo, is practically all we need for such products as cheese and win-

ter apples. On the 22nd of August there sailed out of Montreal another steamer, the ' Bavarian,' and the temperature, as recorded by the thermograph during the voyage, ranged around (SO degrees. During a large portion of the time it was 65 and sometimes as high as 67 degrees. It went down occasionally and intermittently to 55 degrees and 50 degrees, but it immediately rose again, an average difference in temperature of from 5 to 10 per cent between this boat and the ' Canada ' sailing the same day. Then take the ' Mount Temple ' which sailed on the 7th of August; we find that the temperature was at no point lower than 63 degres, ranging most of the time around 65 degrees and 70 degrees and coming out on the other side at 72 degrees.
The next day another boat, the ' Parisian,' sailed the temperature on which at no time was above 65 and ranged from 62 to 65 on all the voyage across. Here we have three steamers crossing the ocean at the same time, and the thermograph records show a very wide difference in the temperature, the only possible way to account for which Is that at least two of them were not properly ventilated. Again, the ' Livonian ' 'sailed on the 5th of June, and on the journey the temperature was as low as 45. At no time did it reach above 60, and that was as she was going down the St. Lawrence. I could quote you numerous other examples of the same kind. Last year the Minister of Agriculture promised that he would provide thermographs in every chamber carrying perishable cargo from Montreal, but if he had done so that would not be sufficient unless there was also a thermograph on the deck. Why has the Minister of Agriculture neglected to have these steamers properly ventilated, when through his neglect the producers of this country lose an enormous sum of money annually by not having their goods landed on the other side in perfect condition. The government have been entirely negligent in this matter, and it is a shame that the people of this country should go on year after year suffering in this way when the government have it in their power so very easily to control the situation. We

have time and again pointed out that something should be done, but for the last seven or eight years the government have been neglectful, and the people have been suffering all that time. It is true that just now the rate for cheese out of Montreal is just as cheap as out of New York, but even now when freight is so scarce, the rate of butter out of Montreal is 43 cents per 100 pounds, while out of New York it is 33 75 cents per 100 pounds, which on our exports of butter last year would have amounted to a loss of $31,450. It is a shame that this enterprising country should have delayed for so long to recognize the value of the St. Lawrence route ; a route which properly utilized and safeguarded would enable us to get the trade not only of the Canadian Northwest but of the American Northwest. This is borne out by our own experience, as we have seen fine fruit turned out of the barrels bruised and unsightly, which were probably a picture to look upon before they began their long journey.
Another objection to the barrel is its size. Grocers have only of late years taken up the sale of imported apples on any scale, and the reason is that they have not always the convenience of stowage required by the barrel, besides which a package containing three bushels of fruit is not a convenient one to handle. The unanimous expression of opinion by this important federation, which represents grocers throughout the entire country, should be taken heed of by shippers in Canada, who, if they can get grocers here to take up the sale of their apples all over the country, need not fear for the disposal of their surplus apples.
The package that would meet the ideas of the grocers here, according to what we have been able to make out from inquiries we have made, is a case of two compartments that would hold about one-half barrel, something after the style of the boxes now arriving from Tasmania and New Zealand. The apples should be laid in tiers, and paper shavings, where these are easily available, would help to prevent bruising and to preserve the flavour of
the fruit, which is mostly gone by the time it gets on our tables.
The barrel is absolutely condemned, and it is to the interests of Canadians to devise some package which shall take its place.
Where does the right lion, gentleman find any justification in that for the negiect of the Department of Agriculture to see that its instructions are properly carried out ?

I do not say that the department has shown any neglect, but I am r.t inting out that there are two or three sides to the question. If Canadian shippers had put their goods in proper packages, an immense number of the complaints that have been advanced would have disappeared. The sending forward of very large quantities in barrels is likely to cause the crushing of the fruit in many cases, particularly if the fruit be of tender character, which must naturally depreciate the products of our orchards when for sale in England. The government are as desirous as hon. gentlemen opposite can be, and have shown every anxiety to advance the interests of the community and of the farmers. So far as there is any justification for the remarks of the hon. gentleman, I am quite sure that my hon. colleague will do his very best to meet any reasonable demand that may be made by the shipping interests in the way of securing better shipments of our products.
These statements from his department as to the steps taken, which I have read, appear to me to show that the department has not been negligent of its duty. It appears to me that the department is doing what it can to provide that these matters shall be carefully attended to. I do not see, Sir, that there is any -very great use, in my hon. friend's (Mr. Fisher's) absence, in prolonging -tins discussion very much. I will call his attention, when he returns, to the speech of the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. E. D. Smith), and to the facts that he has stated-if they be facts ; all I can say is that they do not seem to me to correspond entirely with the statements supplied to me from the Department of Agriculture. I agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. E. 'D. Smith) that the question is of importance ; I agree with him that the attention of the House and the government cannot be called to any subject of more importance than that of seeing to it that all our food products are landed in England in the best possible condition-all that is cor rect and true. The government, and particularly the Department of Agriculture, have been bending their energies in that direction. If, in any respect, they have fallen short or failed, all I can say is that, for one, 1 propose to do my uttermost to remedy these defects. And any one who knows what my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, has done in the past in that direction will agree with me that the hon. gen

tlernan may be relied upon to do all that be can, and the government, too, may be relied upon to do all that they can, to meet the needs and wants of the people in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, when you left the chair at one o'clock we were dealing with the question of cold storage, and were discussing the answer made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who I regret is now not in his place. The minister was excusing the Minister of Agriculture and saying that he was unable to do justice to the subject owing to the absence Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
of his colleague. We regard the Minister of Trade and Commerce as quite as much responsible for any defects in the situation as the Minister of Agriculture, and he should 'have answered for himself rather than for 'the Minister of Agriculture. WThy ? Because the Minister of Trade and Commerce submits and has this House vote subsidies [DOT]for steamships carrying mails. It has always been, we are told, the policy of the government in making these contracts to provide suitable accommodation, cold storage, cool air chambers and ventilated spaces for carrying the products of the country. When we .were giving these subsidies, when parliament was giving consideration for the services of a steamship line, then would have been the best time to impose such conditions to the subsidy as we desired to have attached to It, and it is not and ought not to be the sole aim of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to have this House vote large subsidies to steamships for the purpose of carrying a portion of the mails of this country. He told us that the large bulk of our mails went by New York and would continue to go by New York on account of the more rapid transportation from that port, and because boats leave New York every day, whereas boats leave Montreal and Halifax practically only about once a week. Then if it was only partially for the purpose of carrying mails that the money is given, what was the other purpose ? The other purpose we are told repeatedly by the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce as well, was to induce the v'essel owners to provide suitable cold storage or ventilated chambers for carrying the perishable products of Canada in order to place them on the markets of Europe in the best possible condition. That being the case, whose duty was it above all others to see that this was done, if not that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce ? It was he who got the House to vote the subsidies for these vessels, and who made the contracts with the steamship companies. He was constantly in communication with the steamship companies, and if they failed to make such provisions as would ensure to the people of Canada suitable ventilated chambers and cold storage on these vessels, then they failed to do their duty, and I claim that the Minister of Trade and Commerce *was more responsible than the Minister of Agriculture. When we were discussing 'these subsidies to vessels, his attention was drawn to this state of affairs, and we had the contracts produced: What was the bare provision of the contract? That the companies would provide suitable cold storage with no specifications as to just what provisions should be made and with no authority for the government to supervise or control the system.
This question of ventilation was discussed last year. The Minister of Agriculture was

asked on May 14 about this matter and be answered :
Under this arrangement goods will be put into ordinary holds and they will not be charged any extra but just the ordinary freight rates on the same kind of goods.
He was speaking of the air shafts that were to supply cool air to the hold of the vessel. When the question was asked again across the floor of the House by the hon. member for Wentworth, what charges were made, he answered :
8,796 barrels apples were in cold air chambers and the extra charge was Is. 6d. per barrel.
Now that does not agree with his answer , to us when we were voting the money ; then there was to be no extra charge ; but he says there that it is Is. 6d. per barrel extra, if you take advantage of these cold [DOT]air *chambers. Is that correct ? He assures us in one case that there is no extra charge, and takes credit to himself because they have made that provision in the interests of the farmers of the country, and when the question is put direct to him in another form he says that there is an extra charge for the use of these chambers. The importance of the extra charge of 10 shillings per ton on witter and cheese will be appreciated when I remind the House that the ordinary freight charge is 20 shillings a ton, so that the increase amounts to 50 per cent of the freight charges, for those who take advantage of this arrangement. Whatever benefit might result from the installation of this ventilation was denied to the agriculturists of this country owing to the increased cost.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce said :	Oh, the Minister of Agriculture is
not here. Why did you not bring this up earlier in the session when the Minister -of Agriculture was present ? We have been endeavouring during the whole session up to the last few days to elicit the information we required to enable us to deal with this subject and it was because we could not get this information that we did not bring it up earlier. We had to resort to every expedient in parliamentary practice to obtain that information. We brought it up at the very earliest moment we could so as to enable us to deal with it intelligently and it is not our fault that the hon. Minister of Agriculture is not here. We have had this serious ground of complaint against the government for a long time that generally when these important questions are discussed they are discussed when only one or two or three of the ministers are in the House and when the members of the government charged with the department whose acts are under consideration are nearly always absent. Is it our duty to keep them in the House ? Is it not rather their place to be in the House ? Last night when we were discussing the Public Works estimates
and when we desired information what did the hon. acting minister (Mr. Hyman) tell us ?-it is not in my department ; it is iu the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Then we asked ; Why is not the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefon-taine) here ? This money is being voted ; we want the information to enable us to do our duty to the country properly, to know whether this is a wise vote and if that information can only be got from the Department of Marine and Fisheries why is not the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries here ? I noticed the fact last night that while these important discussions were going on there were only two ministers outside of the ho. minister without portfolio who were in the House, that for a part of the time only one minister was here, and that none of the ministers representing the spending departments of the government that we desired to get information from were here.
How many members of the opposition were present last night ?

There were enough members to put all the questions that we desired to put in order to bring out the information. If the ministers had been here as they ought to have been we could have shortened the time very much and the progress with the estimates would have been much more rapid. I say that we have just ground for complaint and that we have had to complain of the absence of ministers over and over again during the present session. The ministers seem to think that the discharge of their duties in the House is a secondary consideration. We want information but we are told that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries is out. Then, we ask about the Department of Public Works and we are told that the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sutherland) is away, that he is unwell. Then we ask about the Department of Militia and Defence and we are told that the hon. Minister of Militia is not here, next we are told that the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) is not here and we go round from one to the other until we are put to our wits end to know what to do to perform our duty in this House. We cannot get information. For half of the session we have been trying to get information from the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) but we find that that hon. gentleman is rarely here when we are discussing a question in which his department is involved. Where are these men to-day ? Is it our place to compel them to stay here ? Is it rather not their duty tp be here to answer questions put by members of the opposition regarding the conduct of their various departments ? I draw attention to this matter
Order.
I am not a speaking trumpet, and I would like to get an opportunity to say what X have to say-what observation did the Postmaster General make ?
I did not make any observation ; I was only thinking.

I have no objection to your thinking if you and your government would think out how better to discharge your duties. I was proceeding to show that the development of the industry was not due to anything the government had done by providing cold storage, and as proof I drew attention to the fact that only one cheese in fifty-eight was sent in cold storage. The Minister of Agriculture has no right to take to himself the credit for the development of the industry under such circumstances. It is because of these derelictions on the part of the government and because of their lack of intelligence and business foresight that we believe we are justly entitled to move this amendment and to, if possible, censure the government because of the manner in which they have neglected to discharge their duties.
Mr. Speaker-
Oh.

You gentlemen had better keep quiet over there, because you are in cold storage, and you will find it difticuit to get out. There is no use of your sweating ; that is the trouble with the butter and cheese which we send in cold storage ; it sweats. I want to bring the attention of the House and the country to a few things that ought to be understood more fully by the people of Canada. I find in the report of the Minister of Agriculture proof of the most guilty neglect of duty in reference to the condition of our products when they get to the old country. He tells us in his report that in one instance butter shipped to Glasgow in cold storage lay eleven days on the Glasgow dock. What is the use of shipping anything in cold storage when you allow it to be exposed to the weather for eleven days ? There ought to be some business system connected with this cold storage transportation. Previous to the election in 1900, every large rock and boulder through the country was placarded : ' Vote for Laurier and eleven cent cheese.' We are on the rocks now. Then, any poor fellow that got up on a political platform and could not i talk very well, only had to point to the inscription on the rocks. To-day the rocks cry out against the government : Vote for Laurier and seven cent cheese. Where is the won-252
derful accomplishment of the Minister ot Agriculture who himself has to admit that only one box of cheese out of fifty goes in cold storage. It is a strange process of reasoning that will force us to the conclusion that one box of cheese in cold storage will raise the price of the other forty-nine. I call the attention of the country to the further fact that the Canadian farmer to-day is confined to less articles out of which he can make money than ever before in the history of the country. That being so, his butter, his cheese and his cattle must be shipped under proper conditions or he will loose his foothold in the British market. The government are neglecting their duty, and Siberia, New Zealand and Denmark are displacing Canada in the English market. Russia, including Siberia, is taking a larger place in the butter trade of England than Canada is. Talk about what the government has done in the interests of the farmers of Canada. It is the energy of the farmers backed ul>
by the energetic business men of Canada that has pushed the government along. These influences push the cart up the hill and when they get to the top the government shout: ' Look at the load we have drawn.' The Hon. Mr. Fisher is not in his place to-day, but he ought to be ; a farmer should not be away from home in the harvest time. I venture to say, however, Mr. Speaker, that the work won't suffer if he is away, judging of our experience of the man. Until there is a continuity of proper transportation in reference to these perishable products, and provision made on the other shore for their care, our trade will suffer. I am quite willing to admit that it would not be a wise thing for business men, or for the government either to over-ride the business conditions now in control ofl business men in England. But it is possible to use the men in business over there to the interest of this country, and the government have not done that. If the consignee of an article of a Canadian produce of a perishable nature, allows it to remain in Glasgow for eleven days lying on the dock there is a wrong condition of business. I will read what is said in the report of the Agricultural Department for 1903 :
A good deal has been done in recent years to improve the transportation facilities for our export butter trade, so that to-day Canadian butter is carried in cold storage from the time it leaves the creamery until it reaches the British docks. To reap the full advantage of our chain of cold storage transportation it is apparent that the butter should go into cold storage as soon as it is landed in Great Britain.
Why is not that the case ?
Instead of this, however, it is often allowed to remain on the quays at Liverpool and Glasgow several days, greatly to the detriment.

The idea of taking credit for sending butter and cheese over to England in cold storage, and allowing it to lie on the docks there for several days. It makes no difference under what condition you send the article over, if you allow it to stand on the dock until it has deteriorated in value. Can there be any stronger indictment of the government, and particularly the Minister of Agriculture in reference to the cold storage, than this very statement contained in his own report. After all the boasting of hon. gentlemen opposite; taking the last seven years of the Conservative regime and the first seven years of the Liberal regime, the average increase in the price of cheese has only been three-tenths of one cent per pound.
If you take the seven years inclusive of this year, that three-tenths of a cent will be gone ; the average will be less than the average of the seven years previous to the Conservative party going out of power. Then why take such credit to the government ? The song they sing all over the country is : See what we have done for your butter and your cheese ; vote for Laurier and seven-cent cheese. This, as I have said, is on all the rocks. They will not sing the same song this year if they are honest ; they will have to dance to a different kind of music. I want to say this before I sit down. In the interest of these -large products of this country, the condition of the market as affected by the efforts of other people is not duly considered by hon. gentlemen opposite. We are meeting a different condition of things in the English market from what we ever met before, and	until	this	new	condition	is studied	and	met,	the	business	of this
country of that nature cannot be successfully handled. We are too much at the mercy of the efforts of other people in the English market, unless we hold the first place there. ' In order to meet this new condition, it is necessary first to find your market ; and, with all their boasting, hon. gentlemen opposite have not found a new market for this country since they came into power. After having found your market, it is necessary to keep it, and, in order to keep it, it is necessary to suit your market. Unless hon. gentlemen opposite change their system of attending to this business, they will fail to keep their market because they will fail to suit it.

speechtext: At the time he was not qualified but he has since passed his examination, and it is not really necessary now.

It seems to me it would be better for ministers to take men outside the service as their private secretaries. The private secretary to a minister must be mixed up in politics, and I don't think it is well that members of the civil service should take any part in political matters, although of course they should be perfectly free to exercise their franchise.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is something to be said in favour of what my hon. friend urges. But a private secretary, who is acquainted with the details of the department is more useful to the minister than could be an outsider. When Solicitor General, I took the private secretary of my predecessor and found him exceedingly useful. I never had any cause to suspect his loyalty, and when I became Minister of Justice, I took the private secretary of the gentleman whom I succeeded.
Mr. FOWLER, That is all very well, but at the same time a private secretary is bound to mix himself up in politics sometimes.

Administration of Justice - miscellaneous expenditure, including Northwest Territories, $45,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The increase is due to the expanding business of the Northwest Territories. The expenditure has been increasing gradually until it has reached a very large amount. The amount expended in 1902-3 was $42,185. The services which show the largest increases are the maintenance of prisoners and the jury and witness fees, and we are obliged to ask for a supplementary vote of $20,000. making in all the expenditure connected with the administration of Justice in the Northwest Territories some $05,000. The maintenance of prisoners at the police posts costs $26,000. The prisoners who do not go to jail or penitentiary are held over, pending their trial in the mounted police posts, and the mounted police charge the department 60 cents per day for their maintenance. That cost us this year $26,000. Then there is the transport of prisoners from one place to another in the Territories. This is done by the police. We have to pay for the moving expenses and that item amounts to $6,000. Then there are the Crown prosecutors', juries' and witness fees and the coroners and sheriffs' fees.
