speechtext:
I was not present when item 26 was under discussion, bull ,T will take advantage of this opportunity to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to a matter of importance. We have had an admission in this House from an hon. member that he sat here with the expectation of taking a place on the bench in the province of Nova Scotia. Telegrams have been sent by that hon. gentleman to his friendst, petitions have been circulated by his friends with his knowledge among his friends to the senior minister from that province and to the Prime Minister, urging that the hon. gentleman should be given this position on the bench. It was a rule laid down by the late Sir John Macdonald never to give a place upon the bench to any one who asked for it, because any one who asked for this position proved himself thereby utterly unworthy of it. The hon. gentleman to whom I refer is not in his place now. I am sorry he is not. I .will ask the attention of the minister in the meantime, and I will bring it forward again when the hon. gentleman is in his place. I am calling attention to the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell) who has been driven out of every part of Nova Scotia in which he has held any position.
I would ask the Minister of Justice what are the facts in connection with the application of this hon. gentleman for a place on the bench.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No application has been made to me for this position. All I can add to that is that, if I were asked to make a selection for the appointment to the court in the province of Nova Scotia, I do not think that, because of his standing and eminent ability and his position generally,
I could make a better selection than the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell).

I would ask the hon. minister in this connection, why it is that there has been such very great delay in filling the position of chief justice of the province of Nova Scotia ? This has been the subject of a good deal of comment in that province, and the rumour is not by any means unknown that questions of political expediency have had something to do with it;-that is to say, a certain county in the province is a fairly close county in most elections, and that we have had the most unusual condition of a vacancy in the position of head of the highest court of that province continuing now for smething like six months because of that reason, and that reason alone. It is not desirable, in the interest of the administration of justice, that a rumour of that kind should be so common and apparently so well founded as this has been. If I remember rightly the matter was referred to by a question early in the session, and the Minister of Justice said at tne time that the delay in filling the vacancy was due to the fact that the late chief justice still retained the position of judge of the Admiralty Court.

It would not appear to me that that affords any reason whatever for delay In the appointment. In the province of New Brunswick, and elsewhere the gentleman who fills the position of local judge of the Exchequer Court is not the chief justice. That position is not associated in any way with the position of chief justice of Nova Scotia. That position is absolutely distinct from that of the local judge of the Exchequer Court. I know no reason why the Supreme court of Nova Scotia should have been deprived of its head for so many months and cannot conceive of any reason for it. unless we are to assume that the rumours which have undoubtedly been current in the province are worthy of credence. I think it is due to the House as well as to the people of Nova Scotia and especially to the bench and bar of Nova Scotia that my hon. friend should make some statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that the chief justice of Nova Scotia sent in his resignation at the end of January or the beginning of February last. Of course, I speak from recollection only. And at the time he resigned his position as chief justice while retaining his position as judge in admiralty. I quite understand there is no connection between the chief justiceship and the admiralty because the duties of the office of chief justice do not entail the duties of a judge in admiralty. At the same time my hon. friend will realize that it would be advisable in view of the salaries paid-I have to admit, speaking now absolutely for myself, that the salaries are very small,- to offer the position to some one who would enjoy the advantage of being a judge in admiralty and able to add the emoluments derived from that office to these derived from the chief justiceship. The matter has received some consideration and so far no one from Nova Scotia has made complaint that any inconvenience has resulted from the vacancy. Speaking for myself I would" be prepared to urge the appointment of a chief justice. Of course the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) is Aware that the position of chief justice is not under the patronage of the Minister of Justice. The chief justiceships as well as appointments to the Supreme Court are not under the patronage of the Minister of Justice. However, I will see to it, so far as I am concerned, that immediately after the session -we will consider the matter carefully and something will be done towards making the appointment so far as I can arrange.
I do not know the etiquette as to the patronage in regard to these positions, but I believe that the appointment rests with the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That has been the practice since 1885, since Sir John Thompson's time.
It seems to me the Prime Minister should be here to answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not seek to shirk responsibility.
M^r. R. L. BORDEN. Possibly you might leave an item.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You can bring it up at any time..
You will have supplementaries in which that will be touched upon.

I must ask the Minister of Justice to be prepared on some further item to answer this question a little more satisfactorily than he has done to-day. There is no argument at all in what he has said. If the chief justice of Nova Scotia should retain the position of judge in admiralty for the next three years the government of this country would be justified in keeping that position vacant for three years if the argument of the Minister of Justice is a valid one. That is not a valid reason, and it was not believed by the people of Nova Scotia that any such reason has influenced the government. I accept everything the Minister of Justice has said exactly in the sense in which he intended me to understand it. He realizes that perfectly ; I understand it exactly as he intends, but I want him to understand this distinctly that the people of Nova Scotia believe, and I think there is good reason for believing, that the position of chief justice of that province has been kept open for reasons of political expediency and not for the reasons suggested by the Minister of .Justice to-day. It is not right that there should be any dealing with important judicial positions from that standpoint or for reasons of that kind. There are men on the bench and at the bar of Nova Scotia who are not only able but willing to fill that position to-day for the somewhat meagre salary attached to it, and there would have been not the slightest difficulty in filling that position satisfactorily to the people and to the bar of Nova Scotia, without delay of more than one or two weeks after the vacancy occurred. Under these conditions I think it is due to the House that the Minister of Justice should either now or later give some better explanation or that the Prime Minister, if the responsibility devolves on him, should give some better explanation than we have had to-day. The whole matter of judicial appointments may require to be discussed a little either now or later on ; in fact I propose to discuss it. I will not say any more at this time but I would like the Minister of Justice to see that the premier is here when some supplementary estimate of his own is brought before the House in order that this question may be discussed in a more satisfactory way.

In this connection I was a little surprised to hear a gentleman of the standing of the Minister of Justice state that he would have been satisfied to see the member for Hants appointed to a position upon the bench. After the exhibition which was furnished this House and the country yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in defending a gentleman bordering on the condition of a criminal, and his appointment to a high position in the service of this country, I suppose we should be prepared for anything, but I did not think the Minister of Justice would so far forget himself as to endorse the appointment of the hon. gentleman for Hants to a position on the bench. The hon. member for Hants has distinguished himself in this House. He has practically admitted that he is an applicant for the position of chief justice of the province of Nova Scotia. Whether he admits it or hot, it is well known that he is an applicant for the position. It Is well known that he telegraphed the Prime Minister and urged his friends to telegraph the Prime Minister

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will this pass ?
No, we will not pass it while I am on my feet making an arrangement with the Minister of Justice. Under no circumstances will we do that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

The chair should not be discourteous.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have never uttered an uncourteous word in this House in the last four years. Why the hon. member should speak as he has done I do not understand. I must protect myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are two items in the supplementaries for the present year and for the past year. The additional amount required for judges travelling allowances will be found at page 2 of the further supplementary estimates and at page 1 of the supplementaries.
Then I understand that on any of these items this matter may be discussed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On any item, or if it would be more advantageous to have the question widened, we might fix a day on going into supply to take up the matter and discuss it. I will arrange to have the right hon. Prime Minister here and it would probably be better to take it up on going into supply.
Probably it would be better to have it- in committee as there might be some question to be asked and it would be less embarrassing.
Is it the intention of the government or the hon. Minister of Justice to appoint another judge in the Exchequer Court ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That question has been discussed and I must confess I thought it necessary at times to make such an appointment but there is no intention of doing it at the present time.
Then there is no member sitting in this House with the appointment in his pocket ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He may have the appointment but it has not come from me.
Administration of Justice-Yukon Territory, travelling allowance for judges, $1,500.
What allowance for travelling expenses do they require ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The two places at which they sit that I know of are Dawson and Whitehorse. I may say that while we have voted this sum for three years none of it has ever been used.
Living allowance of sheriff, deputy sheriff, clerk of court, assistant clerks, police magistrate and stenographers of territorial court-at $1,800 each, $14,400.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister if Mr. Eilbeclc is yet in the Yukon Territory ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And you are giving him a living allowance in addition to his salary ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: His salary is $4,000 a year and his living allowance $1,800. That is the same living allowance as is paid to all the officials in the Yukon with the exception of the judges who receive $5,000 and the librarian and caretaker who receive each $1,200.

Would it not be better to give them a salary and allow them to live on their salary ? I do not believe in that way of paying officials at all. There is no inducement for them to be economical or to show any respect for the amount of money that you give them. I believe in giving them a proper salary and allowing them to live on their salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think this whole question of living allowance to officials in the Yukon will require to be reconsidered at a very early date but it would be very hard for the Department of Justice to discriminate as against our officials when the officials of other departments are paid living allowances. It is rather a curious anomaly that the officials of other departments who go to Manitoba, the Northwest, the Yukon and British Columbia, are allowed in addition to their salaries certain amounts over and above for living allowances, but the unfortunate judges who happen to be assigned to the courts there are paid actually less salary than they are paid in the eastern provinces.
It is unfortunate but a great many men are very willing to take these positions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The best are not chasing after them.

I understand that the cost of living in the Yukon is not so very much greater than it is in British Columbia. It does seem to me that $5,000 in addition to the salary of a judge is an exceedingly large amount. Not only that, but we make a living allowance of $1,800 a year to the sheriff, deputy sheriff, clerk of court, assistant clerks, police magistrate and stenographers of the territorial court who in addition receive salaries equal to if not greater than those which they would receive if they were occupying the same positions in the eastern provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
At least equal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The sheriff probably gets more than he would receive east but not the rest.
It seems to me that it is about time that kind of thing was stopped.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I agree.
Do I understand the hon. minister to say that the best men are not looking for these positions ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not say that but I did say that they were not made very attractive just now.

Will the hon. minister explain if the judges or officials of his department are on the territorial council and if so, what are their functions ? Are the ordinances of the council laid before this parliament ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think so. I know we receive them. Judge Dugas is on the council but I cannot tell about the others. I think there are six nominative and six elective, or five nominative and five elective members but I do not just remember at the present moment.

That territory is governed and all the record we have of it practically is the voting of the salaries for these officials. There may be records but they have not attracted my attention. Have we any record of the internal rules, regulations and laws that are enforced In the Yukon to-day ? These should be prepared and submitted to parliament at the very earliest date.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will have to look at the Yukon Territory Act which we passed a couple of years ago before I can answer that question. The Act provides for the way in which these ordinances shall be disposed of. I know they come to the department but what is done with them aftar that I do not know.
The stenographers are paid salaries greatly in excess of what similar officers in the east receive.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They get $2,000 a year.

The court stenographers in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia do not get any such salaries, and I doubt if they do in Ontario. In addition to the $2,000 you give the Yukon stenographers $1,800 living allowance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In Quebec the stenographers are paid by fees, and these fees are such as to enable them to earn very much more than $2,000 a year. The work of a stenographer is very hard work indeed. A man who is obliged to attend in court all day and do this work earns every dollar he gets, and I can quite appreciate that $2,000 for a really good stenographer- there are two of them up there

is not too much.
It is not too much if they are good men.

That all depends upon the amount of labour they perform, and the frequency of the court sittings. It may be that the work of these stenographers is very light indeed, and it need not follow that they must be of the expert class.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know Mr. Craig, but I do know Mr. Yaliquette ; he is an Irishman with a French name which reverses the usual order and he is expert in both English and French.
He ought to be paid double then.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The police court stenographer only receives $1,200.

I am not objecting to the $2,000, but I do object to the living allowance of $1,800 which brings the salary up to $3,800 a year. We have official reporters in this House who perform duties very much more onerous than the gentlemen in the courts in the Yukon, and our reporters get just the same salary of $2,000, and as I understand they have to pay their own living allowance.

I would like to suggest to the Minister of Justice the propriety of having both the stenographers and the sheriff paid by fees.
At these salaries, these men are probably getting from $50 to $75 a day for every day they work. The stenographers cannot be working in court all the time, and I think it would be better to compensate them by fees which of course considering the conditions in the Yukon might be higher than they are in the east; I do not think we should pay them $3,800 a year, for perhaps not working a quarter of the year. I would draw the attention of the minister to the fact that the Yukon judges are getting in living allowance and salary, twice what the judges get in Ontario. The Yukon jud-Mr. FITZPATRICK.
ges get $5,000 salary and $5,000 living allowance. Living is pretty expensive now in Ontario, as the government points out when they propose to increase the salaries of civil servants. The judges of the High Court in Ontario get $5,000 salary and they have to live on that. I would assume that the Ontario judges are at least equally as competent jurists as the judges in the Yukon. It would be better in my opinion to give the Yukon judges a salary and let them live economically, or extravagantly as they think fit. It would be a more businesslike way of dealing with the matter. I would not be penurious ; I would give them a good salary, but I do not believe in giving half of the stipend in the name of salary and the other half as living allowance: It would indicate that he is supposed to save his salary and live on the allowance. In Ontario a stenographer gets $5 a day when he sits in court and so much per folio for the evidence transcribed, and they manage to make a pretty good income out of it, but they earn all they get and they are busy most of the time. It would be more satisfactory, I think, if the stenographers were paid by fees.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If this question of living allowance is to be reconsidered I would like to have it reconsidered in a general way in regard to all the departments, and not to have my department singled out especially. I had an idea at the time the Yukon judges were appointed, that it was not proper to give them this living allowance, but the difficulty arose that if we paid a judge in the Yukon a higher salary than his brother judge elsewhere, and if we wanted to transfer him to another part of the country, he would be sitting side by side with another judge who had far *less salary, but who would be performing the same duty. The same difficulty would arise on the retirement of a Yukon judge. I certainly am not of opinion that exorbitant salaries should be paid ; the salaries are large enough already ; they are quite generous. Remember that I am now speaking of the Yukon and not of other parts of the country, because so far as other parts of Canada are concerned I wish to make it quite clear, speaking for myself, that in my opinion the whole question of judicial salaries requires consideration at the earliest possible moment. 1
Hear, hear.
Would not the salary attach to the office and not to the man ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is attached to I he man. We pass a statute providing for the appointment of a judge, and in the same statute we provided for the salary, so that he that takes the position takes the salary.
Even if he were sent somewhere else ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, that is the difficulty.
Do any of these officials get fees in addition to their salaries ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, the Crown prosecutor is paid by fees.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What about the sheriff ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The sheriff gets his salary, I am opposed to the system of fees to sheriffs and clerks of the court. I believe, generally speaking, that the fees should go into the public exchequer, and that the man should get his salary. Otherwise, especially when they are far away from control, you could not tell what might happen.
I agree with that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I hope the Minister of Justice will give instructions that the sheriff of the Yukon will confine his electioneering to the Yukon territory in the coming elections, and that he won't send him down to Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I never did. I do not approve of it in any manner, shape or form.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Then we will take for granted that he will stay at home this time.
Yukon Territory-law books, &c., and freight thereon, for the use of the bench and bar, and stationery, and freight thereon, for use of courts, $2,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So far as I am concerned, this is the last year provision will be made for the library up there. It must be far enough advanced now for them to maintain their own library.
Yukon Territory-miscellaneous expenditure, .including fees and expenses of Crown prosecutor, salary and living allowance of stenographer of police court and other officials or employees connected with the administration of justice, coroners' inquests, &c., &c., $25,000.

speechtext: We spent last year $19,480.64.

What pay does a constable in the Dominion Police receive now ? They are a very fine body of men.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think they get from $1.50 to $1.90. I think $2.10 is paid to inspectors.

That is a pretty small wage considering the cost of living in the capital. I think the minister might reasonably give some small increase to these men. The constables in most of the towns of Ontario get more than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think after three years they get $1.90. I can say, as the official head of the department, that these men are admirably well qualified, and they deserve every possible consideration. They are certainly as fine a body of men as we can possibly have. I may say that no department of the government is administered with less friction and gives the minister less trouble than the Dominion Police.

The best expression of the appreciation of the minister would be a slight increase in the salaries of these men.
Kingston Penitentiary, $177,600.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Last year the Minister ot Justice stated, in reference to the chaplain of Kingston penitentiary, that he purposed making an arrangement by which each denomination should,take week or month about to fill the position, which was then vacant. Has that been carried out ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was said when the Bill for the amendment of the Penitentiaries Act was up last year. My hon. friend will remember that the Bill was dropped. That appeared to be the unanimous desire of the House, so far. as I could gather at the time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What action was taken ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Bill was dropped and nothing was done. The old order of things was allowed to continue.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I have a letter from a clergyman in Kingston, which reads as follows :
Permit me to report to you as a member of parliament what quite a few in these parts regard as a high-handed way of making government appointments. In a few brief words permit me to state the case. The Rev. Cartwright, brother of Sir Richard, and an Episcopalian, has been chaplain in the penitentiary for twenty-five years. Lately he decided to resign. His resignation was accepted and Rev. Cooke, an Episcopalian, was installed as chaplain without any person knowing anything about the change. One of the executive told me to-day that as an executive they knew nothing about the change until they saw it published in the city papers. Now, what many of us object to is this stealthy way of filling important government positions of this character without giving other denominations any opportunity of having a represen-

tative apply tor the position. I will be glad if you can do anything which will open the whole case so that th.e appointment can be made in the light of day and not inside prison walls.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would my hon. friend pardon me if I ask him to explain the word ' executive ' in that letter ? I do not understand what that means.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Neither do I.
That would be the local executive of the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I allow politics to run a great many things, but I do not allow it to run religious matters.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister has not carried out the arrangement he spoke of last year, but, on the recommendation of the executive committee of the Liberal party in Kingston, this gentleman was appointed at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think my hon friend is quite wrong. The statement in the letter he read was to the effect that the executive had not been consulted in regard to the appointment.
Was any recommendation received as to the minister appointed ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only person I would consult as to the appointment of a chaplain belonging to the Episcopal Church would be the bishop.
Was any recommendation received from anybody else ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not remember.
Who recommended the appointment ? Was the recommendation received from the executive of the Liberal party ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly not, 1 would not consult them in such a matter.
Was he appointed on the recommendation of the bishop ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot say, but if I consulted anybody, he would be the only one.
Then there was no one consulted ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not that I can recollect.
There wore some recommendations, however, received by the' department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no recollection of any.
Would it be possible to ascertain from the tiles of the department from whom the recommendations came ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will see.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: And we will have an opportunity of discussing the matter later ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If this were a question of the appointment of a Roman Catholic chaplain, I should not like to discuss the question of recommendations. I would rely absolutely and exclusively on the question of fitness. I do not like, so far as the appointment of a chaplain is concerned, to discuss the question of recommendations.
That is just the reason why I ask the minister to bring uown all the communications with his department with respect to the appointment of this gentleman to the position of chaplain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will consider that.
I understand the hon. gentleman to agree to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will consider it. I would not like to establish the precedent.

If the position which the minister takes is a sound one, if he would not consider any recommendations made, there can be no objection to his bringing tnese down, so that rve may see what recommendations were made and who made them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The particular point I made, and it is quite apparent to anybody, is that the executive of the Liberal party was not consulted. So far as I am concerned, I would not consult it in a matter of that description.
WThat is the rule in the case of Protestant chaplains ? Are they confined to any particular denomination ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. At New Westminster the chaplain is a Presbyterian. In Manitoba he is a Methodist and at Kingston, St. Vincent de Paul and Dorchester, the Protestant chaplains are Anglican.
What about the Salvation Army ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You can leave them, to me. They do the work outside the gates and do it very effectively. I have an item in the estimates for them.
I understand the minister to say that this appointment was not made on the recommendations or the Lord Bishop of Kingston.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If I were appointing a Roman Catholic chaplain. I would make the appointment on the recommendation of the Archbishop. In the case of the Reverend Mr. Cook, I cannot recollect whether or not he was appointed on the recommendation of his bishop, but I have grave doubts about it. The only man I would consult in the case of that kind, and the only one I think, would be entitled to be consult-

etl would be the ecclesiastical superior of the chaplain.
Was he consulted ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot say.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It would be better if the Minister of Justice would carry out the statement he made last year with reference to the Protestant chaplains. He said that all denominations should have a representative. At Kingston there is a Roman Catholic and there is also a Presbyterian. I have no objection to that, but the other denominations should be represented.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps they are not represented in the penitentiaries.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Are you sure 1 made that statement ? Of course I will take my hon. friend's word for it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am sure that was the statement made. If the hon. minister will look up ' Hansard ' he will find it there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The law provides for one Catholic and one Protestant chaplain.
Dorchester penitentiary, $59,700.

speechtext:

llr. FITZPATRICK. Two years ago, 1 allowed one 2nd class clerkship to drop. It had been held by Mr. Blackadar. I wish to recreate that clerkship intending to appoint Miss Armstrong, who has been for many years in the department and who is a very competent person. [DOT]

speechtext:
Mr. Creighto1!! was accountant of the Kingston penitentiary. A few years ago I transferred the book-keeping of the penitentiary to this department here and brought Mr. Creighton to Ottawa. He has proved such an efficient man that I wish to increase his salary $200.

Borden) wishes to bring up the question of the judges' salaries.
Administration of justice-penitentiaries generally-to pay expenses in connection with supervision of paroled and discharged convicts, $2,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is a new departure for which I ask the approval of the House. In connection with the paroled conI victs we find that a great number fall away to their old habits because they cannot get employment or assistance. This is an item put in.at the suggestion of Superintendent Archibald, of the Salvation Army, who has done an immense amount of good in connection with the prison-gate work of the Salvation Army. The Army has a certain number of people who attend at the prison gate-they know when men are to be released, being kept informed when they inquire by the Department of Justice-and they take hold of these men, find them employment, help them along and encourage them. If a man, for instance, is a mechanic, and needs tools, or something of that kind, the intention is that Superintendent Archibald may be able to take out of this fund such an amount as is necessary to help the chap along. I find that it is absolutely necessary to give a man a chance, if he has happened to fall into trouble and the best way when he gets out of gaol, is for society not to turn its back upon him.
Hear, hear.

I thoroughly endorse what the minister has said and am very glad that he has this vote in the estimates. There are none more worthy of assistance and none

Unit are doing better work for the poorer *classes than the Salvation Army. I think the minister will remember that last session we had a little talk about it. I think that all parties in this House and out of it will endorse the passing of this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Inspector draws my attention to the fact that, perhaps, under the item as it appears in the 'estimates we may not be able to do all we want. He suggests, therefore, that it should be amended so that we may be able to buy a kit for a discharged convict or anything of that kind. I would move that it be amended to read, ' travelling expenses and aid to discharged convicts. ' That will make it absolutely clear.
Amendment agreed to.
Why not say that this is for the Salvation Army ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: 'No, I always mean what I say, and I think that here I have said what I mean. This vote is put in at the request of Mr. Archibald, I want, if I can- I am not sure I. shall be able to do it-to appoint an officer who will receive a salary to do this work. I tried to get Superintendent Archibald, but the Salvation Army would not let him go.
Will the new officer be a Salvation Army man ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is my inclination.
The minister keeps a register of those who are on parole and how they turn out afterwards ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. It may be of interest to the committee to know that there are eight men who are discharged convicts from the penitentiary-I will not say where they are, but the facts are given me by Superintendent Archibald-who have been placed by him in important positiohs of trust. One of them has held his position for five years. The employer knows that he is a discharged convict, but no one else knows it. Not one of these men has fallen away.
Hear, hear.
Can the hon. minister give us the returns of those who have been paroled and who have broken their parole ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will find that in my report. I will look it up in a moment.
Did the minister agree [DOT]on this amount with the Salvation Army ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I am glad to see this item in the estimates. The only reason I wish to speak about it is that I wish to say a word about Superintendent Archibald. If the minister can secure his services, he will Mr. WILSON.
have the best man in all Canada for this work. I have had the advantage and privilege of knowing Superintendent Archibald from boyhood. He is a splendid specimen of manhood and, as I say, the best man the minister could have for carrying on this work.

I find the parole system operates admirably, and if I were connected with this work for any great number of years I would adopt the Swiss system in reference to the sentence, the indeterminate sentence so that a man in jail would feel that on his own good conduct would depend the time of his release.

I am glad to hear this is turning out so well. I know that the hon. gentleman's predecessor Mr. Mills was much in favour of it and I thought he was right, but I have seen some adverse criticisms of the system since that, indicating that if the system was not being abused, it was at any rate not turning out as great a success as was anticipated. The minister speaks of the inspectors. How many inspectors of penitentiaries are there at present ?

speechtext: There are two.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He remains an inspector. He is the senior inspector but remains in the department constantly at my disposal. The other is Mr. Dawson. Previous to the appointment of Mr. Dawson the penitentiary of British Columbia had not been inspected for three years.
You have a good man there.

The explanation is:
Manitoba-to pay cost of transfer of 32 prisoners to St. Vincent de Paul, $1,500 ; cost of brick-making plant and necessary buildings, $2,500 ; maintenance of convict population above that estimated $1,000. Is this brick plant in Manitoba bought to manufacture the brick you want for your own use ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. There are two things to be borne in mind in a prison expenditure of this kind. First, you have to provide employment for the inmates, and second, to utilize the product after manufacture. We have to add a wing to the building and the brick will he utilized in that way. We have also to build a fence or wall around it and we find that it will be cheaper to buy and install a plant at the cost of $2,500. You must remember that as it is very much cheaper to manufacture your bricks in Manitoba than to buy them in the market. I am told that in Manitoba brick costs $12 a thousand delivered at the penitentiary. It can be manufactured for very much less than that.

Consolidation of Dominion statutes which may be paid, notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act or in the Act respecting the Department of Public Printing and Stationery, $20,000.
I wish to ask the hon. minister when the consolidation of the statutes will be completed, what it will cost, and why there has been so great a delay ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There has not been any very great delay in the statute revision. The appointment of the commissioners were made only a little over a year ago, and the result is that the statute revision is now practically completed, with the exception of the following public Acts : Criminal Code. Interpretation, Dominion Notes, Militia (which we are now considering), Northwest Mounted Police, Provincial Subsidies, Statistics, Reformatories, Dominion Police, Bills of Exchange, Banks and Banking, Insurance, Evidence, Extradition and Fugitive Offenders' Acts. All the rest are done. There is no reason why we should not be able to get through with the revision of the statutes within a reasonable time, probably within the next three or four months. The commissioners are :	Sir Henry Strong, chairman : Mr. E. L. Newcombe, Deputy Minister of Justice : Mr. Aug. Power, chief clerk, Department of Justice : Mr. E, R. Cameron, Registrar of the Supreme Court ; Mr. Henry Robertson, of Coliingwood ; Mr. Thomas B. Metcalfe. Winnipeg : Mr. W. E. Roscoe, Kentville; and Mr. L. P. Sirois, Quebec.

The expenditure up to the present time for printing, stationery, salaries of commissioners and salaries of clerks is $33,146.
What will the total cost be ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The total cost ought to he, although this does not provide for the final printing, in the neighbourhood of $40,000. The last revision in 1886 cost $46,049. I imagine we ought to remain within that figure.
Do you include the printing in the $46,000 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. The salaries in 1886 amounted to $46,049.
Do the gentlemen in the department get special pay for this ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They get some pay.
Do they not get as much as the others ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
Explain why, and what they do. .

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will explain, in the first instance, the reason why we are employing these permanent officials. The Deputy Minister of Justice is constantly advising in respect to the construction of these statutes, he is an expert draughtsman, he is absolutely expert in the art of drafting, and he has enormous experience in so far as the statutes in respect to the different departments are concerned. I have handed over all these statutes to him.
What kind of a man is Mr. Power ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Power has been in the department since 1871. He is one of the oldest officials in the department. He is a gentleman who is connected with the consideration of appeals in respect to criminal matters. They are dealt with by him. He is also a very competent draughtsman, is a member of the bar of Quebec, has a very good knowledge of French, and is of very great assistance in the revision of the statutes.
A pretty old man.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Men, like wine, improve with age. Mr. Newcombe gets $1,500 and Mr. Power gets $1,000, the intention being that they should give their own time after office hours to this work.
How much do commis sioners like Mr. Robertson, for instance, get ?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The salaries of these gentlemen have not been fixed, because my intention was to make some sort of a distribution, so far as they were concerned, in | proportion to the amount of work done, and Mr. FITZPATRICK.
I will make my intention clear when I explain how they proceed. Each man takes home with him a certain number of statutes, does the work, after which the commissioners meet. There have been three meetings up to the present time in Ottawa. At these meetings each man's work is revised by some other members of the commission, and then there is a sub-committee composed of Mr. Newcombe, Mr. Roscoe and Mr. Sirols, who take the work of the general commission and give a finishing touch to it, and I accept the work of this sub-committee as the final revision. I am one of those who believe that there is not always wisdom in numbers in so far as the drafting of statutes is concerned, and I think that by leaving the matter in the hands of a sub-committee we will probably have the matter disposed of more satisfactorily, and in the end we shall have better work. A clear understanding was arrived at with the commissioners that . roue of them is to receive over $4,000.
How much does Sir Henry Strong get ?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He gets $3,500. i will give the amounts that have been paid to each: Mr. Newcombe, $2,000; Mr. Power. $1,700 ; Mr. Cameron, $1,700 ; Mr. Robertson, $1,600 ; Mr. Metcalfe, $1,600 ; Mr. Ros coe, $3,200 ; Mr. Sirois, $2,100.
They are to receive the sum of $4,000 as the total amount ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, as the tota: amount.
After the last revision I think one or two copies of the statutes were supplied to each member of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Each member ought to be entitled to three copies.
I do not understand fhe functions of the Printing Bureau.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, do not ask me to explain them. I am never able to get anything done there.
Are these statutes printed in the Printing Bureau ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes ; they have to be done there.
Expenses of litigated matters which may be paid for services in connection with the litigation conducted within the Department or Justice, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $15,000.
How much was spent of this last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Somewhere in the vicinity of $12,000.
Is it counsel fees principally ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. As a result of the change that has taken place since the

deputy minister has undertaken to look after litigated matters, 1 may mention that while for instance in 1897 the cost amounted to $101,000, last year we decreased them to $72,000. In the amount paid to lawyers in the city of Ottawa it is now down to $5,000 lrom $16,000 to $19,000 previously. I say this to the credit of the officers of the Justice Department, and not for any other purpose.
Where was the rest of it spent ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All over the Dominion. When a lawyer is employed in my department as a rule the department pairs, but at times there are payments for opinions taken by the Department of Justice itself and they come out of the $15,000.
What rule guides you as to the payment of counsel fees ? Is it the rule of thumb ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Gisborne is the taxing officer of the department. He . has been there for a great number of years, and he is almost like the man who sleeps with a gun between his arms.
Like Alexander Mackenzie.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And he got no thanks for it either.
As far as the smallness of the fees go it is dog eat dog.

I had a lot of experience with Mr. Gisborne and he allows about half what an ordinary taxing master in the province would. It is very seldom that I have a grievance, but I have a grievance now, and it is the grievance of some [DOT] Liberals in my county more than my own. I and some Liberal lawyers filed six or eight petitions of right in connection with the Belmont accident on the Intercolonial Railway. We desired not to raise the question of negligence. I' agreed with my learned friend, Mr Mackenzie and other Liberal lawyers well known to the Prime Minister who were engaged in this suit, to have petitions of right tiled. There were cases of great hardship in this Belmont accident. My learned friend Mr. Mackenzie, a very eminent Liberal in the constituency and n very good man, filed a petition in one case of great hardship. I may mention that Mr. Mackenzie frequently praises Sir Wilfrid Laurier all through the constituency, and his praises of Sir Wilfrid Laurier is the greatest difficulty I met with in getting certain electors to vote for me. This good Liberal, Mr. Mackenzie, joined with me in saying that these Belmont claims should be settled in some way by the government without litigation. The claimants are mostly widows with large families, whose husbands were killed in the accident. These petitions of right were filed with the Minis
ter of Justice some months ago, and they were referred to the Railway Department, but since then we have heardnothing of them. I had a letter from Mr. Mackenzie asking me to get Mr. Sinclair and other Liberal members to call upon the minister, and ask him if he would not agree to give those people a reasonable indemnity without sending them to the Exchequer Court. That indemnity could be included in the estimates of this year and the claimants paid. Several of these cases are of particular hardship. I told Mr. Mackenzie that he should write to Mr. Laurier about the case in which he is interested-
An lion. MEMBER. Sir Wilfrid Laurier.

I beg pardon ; it makes no difference with a democrat up to the hilt.
Som hon. MEMBERS. Hear. hear.

In the case in which Mr. Mackenzie is interested a man named Wall who had a family of six children, was killed, and the whole of his family are now depending on their friends. I would ask. Mr. Emmerson, the Minister of Justice to treat these people generously, and to place some reasonable compensation for them in the estimates. They are poor people ; too poor to take their cases to court unless the government dispenses some measure of generosity, it means an absolute denial of justice to the sufferers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When these applications are made to the Department of Justice we have absolutely no power to dispose of them until such time as the department interested is heard from. I act merely as the legal adviser of each department, and therefore it is for the Railway Department to consider as to whether or not they would test the suit or settle. If my hon. friend (Mr. Gourley) will be good enough to call around to see me to-morrow morning we might take the matter up and after we have had a discussion together, I may be able to make representations in the proper quarter, and try to come to a settlement.
I shall be glad to. I thank the Minister of Justice.

Sometimes great injustice is done in the Railway Department in connection with these accidents on the Intercolonial Railway. At Norton an old lady and her daughter coming from early church, were driving, in a closed buggy across the track, and as trains do not usually run in our province on Sunday, they were I not expecting a train to come along and I they were instantly killed. The Railway I Department reported there was no liability , and they did not seem to think there was even any moral claim. These people were , too poor to go to law, and the result is that justice is denied them.

To pay claims for losses of property destroyed by fire rendered necessary to secure the recapture without loss of life, of escaped convict, Ernest Cashel ffm. Pitman, jr., $675 ; G. H. Pitman, $100 ; Thos. Emery, $50 ; A. B. Choate, $25-$850.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The explanation of this appropriation is ns follows : There was a convict of the name of Ernest Cashel under sentence of death in the guard room at Calgary. On the 10th of December he escaped. Somebody had furnished him with revolvers, and he overpowered the guard. He was immediately followed by the police, but he was not captured until the 24th of January. During that period so close was the pursuit that he did not get more than twelve or fifteen miles from Calgary. After a chase of more than thirty days, he was located at a certain point. On a*Sunday morning he was found by the police hiding in a hillock. When he saw the police, he took refuge in the cellar of a log cabin belonging Jo one Pitman, and commenced firing on the police. In order to save life, the police got the permission ot Pitman to set fire to the building and smoke him out, which they did, and he had to come out and surrender. This vote is to compensate Pitman and those who were with him for the losses they sustained- Pitman himself as the owner of the property, and his relatives, one named Emery and one named Choate. Pitman lost his house and the others their clothing and other property. They asked for compensation to the amount of $1,450. The claim was referred to the mounted police and the Crown prosecutor at Calgary, and this settlement was agreed upon.
Are the constables who were overpowered by this man still in the force ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. There were three men, who, I am sorry to say, were guilty of something very unusual. They allowed themselves to be bulldozed by this man and covered, who covered them with his revolver. They have all been dismissed from the service, and two of them are in jail for some technical offence.
Were they suspected of a desire to assist Cashel to escape ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I think not. I think the escape was the result of loose discipline on the part of one of the officers, who has been reprimanded for it. He is a very good officer, and I would not like to mention his name. But the best of men will sometimes make a mistake, and he did not pay sufficient attention to a warning which had been given to him that Cashel had communication with people outside. Instead of taking the precaution to have a sufficient guard put over him, he disregarded the warning.
Why, then, punish the three constables who never heard of this warning ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Because the constables were guilty of cowardice.
That is all very fine, when perhaps the constables were standing in the corridor unarmed. It seems that the officer was warned, and yet did not warn his men.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. The superintendent was warned by two of the inspectors that they had reason to suspect that there were communications with Cashel from the outside ; and there were, because he had two revolvers in his possession. But when Cashel chose his moment, there were three officers in the guard-room. It was their duty to be on guard, and. even if unarmed, not to surrender, but to risk their lives.' They were guilty of such conduct as I think, for the honour of the force, which is above reproach, should not be tolerated.
To pay amount of reward offered for the recapture of escaped convict, Ernest Cashel, $1,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This explains itself. We offered a reward of $1,000 for such information as would lead to the recapture of Cashel.
Who gets the reward?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It has not been decided yet. There are several claimants.
The newspaper reports showed that there were a number of ranchers in the locality who rendered very valuable services to the police force.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
So there were.
To compensate members of the Northwest mounted police for injuries sustained while i in the performance of duty, $1,500.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This requires some explanation. To the men who suffer from accidents in the service such as loss of limbs or wounds, if they are disabled in any way, we give pensions varying from sixteen cents to sixty cents a day. At the present time we have nineteen beneficiaries, and the amount we paid last year in that connection was $1,923.55. Sometimes it happens that a man is disabled in early life, and instead of receiving the pension he makes application for a lump sum. For instance, there is a man thirty-three years of age who receives a pension of thirty cents a day, having received an injury to ihis foot. He has asked to have his pension commuted to a cash sum of $800. The controller of the mounted police submitted a case based on this man's age to the super-

intendent of insurance, who replied that, upon the British mortality tables and at 34 per cent interest, the commuted value of the pension would be $1,540. The man is willing to take a lump sum of $800. It is to deal w'ith such cases that we take this appropriation.
If the man is entitled to $1,500, 1 do not think you should cut him off with $800.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The man has asked for $800, and we are willing to give him that, provided it is within the commutation tables.

The present value of the pension, reduced to capital, is $1,500. We have sometimes to legislate to protect men igainst themselves, and if this man has suffered such an injury as to entitle him to $1,500, he should be paid that much even though he is willing to take less. You should not take advantage of him.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We are not taking advantage of the man. He is able to look after his own business, and he offers o take a cash sum of $800. Therefore we think we should give him that, and no more.

I would again draw the First Minister's attention to the fact that the mounted police who did duty in he Northwest in 1885, have never received my recognition in the way of land scrip, as other officers and men did. t is not too late yet, and I am satisfied that he right hon. the First Minister will only lo himself and the splendid force of which ic has the honour to be the head simple ustice in giving these men the same recog-dtion as was given alll the others in the northwest, namely, 160 acres of land.
Sir WILFRip LAURIER. This takes us >ack to 1885. After the rebellion the gov-rn-ment of the late Sir John Macdonald, vhich was then in office, considered the case if the volunteers and the mounted police, nd decided to give scrip to the volunteers nd not to the mounted police. The reason hey made this discrimination was that the olunteers were men who left their civil vocations to serve their country, and the [DOT]overnment of that day thought it only pro-ier that they should have a -special reward, vhereas the mounted police were profes-ional soldiers, whose engagement it was to erve their country whenever called upon, nd who, consequently, were only carrying ut their ordinary avocation when they went o the front. GALLIHER moved that the amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 79) to incorporate the Thompson River Improvement Company be concurred in.

I notice that the amendments to this Bill are very extensive, several clauses have been wholly cut out and others considerably changed. We have not had opportunity to examine these amendments and, if they are to be gone on with, some one should explain their nature and effect.

The Bill stands in the name of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Morrison), but it is really a Bill introduced by myself. The Bill was modelled on an Act of last session relating to the Columbia River Improvement Company. In going through the Private Bills Committee of this House one section of the Bill with regard to the schedules was left out. Practically, the rest of the Bill was left the same as the other. It then went to the Senate, where some objections were raised to it by parties in the neighbourhood of the Thompson river around Kamloops. They were represented before the Private Bills Committee of the -Senate by a lawyer from Kamloops. Finally, certain amendments were agreed to by both parties, and so the Bill was made satisfactory to those who were objecting as well as the promoters. After that, the Senate made some further amendments, and the Bill comes before us with all these changes in it. I do not know whether there is any objection to the amendments made by the Senate. But I know that the session is far advanced, and it seems to me the Bill ought to be considered to-night and assented to. It is a Bill, I believe, that is in the interest of the whole lumber industry along the North Thompson river. Parties are putting a great deal of money into that industry. Naturally, Bills of this kind arouse the opposition of some

parties, probably for personal reasons. These may be very good reasons ; but, since the two parties interested in the question came before the Senate and agreed, it seems to me that no objection should be made here, unless it can be shown that some of the clauses are objectionable.

The amendments are so extensive that I contend no one on the spur of the moment can go over them carefully and learn what is the effect of them. I do not think that the argument that the session is far advanced and that therefore we ought to pass the Bill right or wrong should carry much weight. Nor do I think that the argument is conclusive that two parties who claim to be interested have agreed upon this Bill. All that part of the country may be interested and we here are the persons who are supposed to be looking after their rights. Because the conflicting interests of two lumbering concerns have been accommodated, it does not follow that the House should accept the division of interest that they have made. This is not to say that I have noticed anything in the Bill specially objectionable. But the amendments are extensive and I think that some little time should be given to consider them ; we should have time to look over them and see whether they should be made.
We have an hour to consider this Bill, and I do not see anything iu the nature of the amendments that would make it necessary to spend longer time upon it
I think the hon. gentleman might leave it until the next sitting of the House.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) can have it brought up on Monday.

There are some parties here who are waiting to see the Bill through. For my part I do not see why the Bill cannot be taken up and the amendments read and considered now. We have an hour to do it, so why should it be postponed ? I do not usually press these matters, and If there were other private Bills to occupy the hour to be devoted to that order of business, I probably would not press it now. But, why cannot we consider it within the time ?
Mr. SPROULE/. The hoh. gentleman surely does not want to keep the House held "up while we are going through these amendments.
If the House were never held up in a worse cause than in considering whether this Bill is right or wrong, no one would have cause to grumble.
These amendments came suddenly upon us and we have had no time to give them such examination as

would have been given in the Committee on Private Bills. I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) should allow this Bill to stand over until Monday and, in the meantime, let some department of the government examine these amendments carefully and state to the House whether this Bill should be passed or not. If the government take the responsibility, it will go a long way towards removing any objection that might otherwise be made. I do not wish to detain the House for an hour to go into the Bill, for there is other business that might better occupy our attention.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the committee, I am sure, has not forgotten that last year we sent an expedition to explore, patrol and assert the authority of the government of Canada in Hudson's Bay and

the northern waters. The object of this expedition was fully explained to the House last year and met with general favour. Thq view was to assert beyond any possibility of doubt, so as to prevent any future possible conflict, the undoubted authority of the Dominion of Canada in the waters of Hudson's Bay and beyond. The steamer ' Neptune ' was chartered last year and sailed from Halifax. It had on board a representative of the Geological Department, a representative of the Marine and Fisheries Department, Inspector Moodie and five men of the mounted police. The expedition for the time being was under the chief control of Mr. Lowe. He was to explore, as far as he could during the season, the northern waters and to establish a post somewhere in Hudson's Bay. No definite instructions were given to the expedition as to the location of the post. Then, as soon as the break of the ice in the spring would permit, the expedition was to go north and explore Baffin Bay and Lancaster iStrait, and then come back to Cape Chidley, on the Straits of Hudson Bay. There they would be met by another boat, wihich was to sail, and has sailed on the loth of July to meet them, give them coal, provisions, &c. The 'Neptune Ms to come back and be relieved and be replaced by another boat, the ' Arctic,' which will be under the command of Captain Bernier, and which is to sail on August 15. This boat will carry an officer and ten men of the mounted police, apart from the crew of the ship. They will relieve the ' Neptune.' Their instructions are to patrol the waters, to And suitable locations for posts, to establish those posts and to assert the jurisdiction of Canada. The government has been induced to come to this action because it is evident that the time has come when our interests in these northern waters should not longer be neglected. At the present time there are whalers and fishermen of different nations cruising in those waters, and unless we take active steps to assert, what is the undoubted fact, that these lands belong to Canada, we may perhaps find ourselves later on in the face of serious complications. Perhaps the committee would understand it better if I should point out on the map the proposed routes of these vessels, and the places which I have mentioned.
Towards the erection of a monument to Champlain at St. John, $5,000.

Mr. Chairman, I am not objecting to this item at all, but I raised a question in this House some little time ago in regard to the erection of a monument to the memory of the late Hon. Thos. D'Arcy McGee. Has the right hon. Prime Minister considered that question ? While I am not objecting to the erection of a monument to the memory of Champlain I think that the late Hon. Thos. D'Arcy McGee is entitled to some consideration at the hands of the government.
253i
Sir WILFRID LAtTRIER. Hear, hear.
And I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has considered the question and if there will be something in the estimates this year for the purpose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am afraid that there will be nothing in the estimates this year but this is an idea which will not escape our memory another time.
Is there any special reason why this monument should be placed at St. John ?
He landed there.
Do X understand that Champlain suggested the Trent canal also ?

Yes, be is partly responsible for it. Parkman continues :
It was the eighth of September, and Champlain, shivering in his blanket, awoke to see the bordering meadows sparkling with an early frost, soon to vanish under the bright autumnal sun. The Huron fleet pursued its course along the bosom of Lake Simcoe, up the Little River Talbot, across the portage to Balsam lake, and down the chain of lakes which form the sources of the River Trent. As the long line of canoes moved on its devious way, no human life was seen, no sign of friend or foe, yet, at times, to the fancy of Champlain, the borders1 of the stream seemed decked with groves and shrubbery by the hands of man, and mighty walnut trees, laced with grape-vines, seemed decorations of a pleasure-ground.
Trees and grape-vines similar to those which Champlain gazed upon are to be seen there to-day. Then, Parkman goes on to describe the adventures, battles and hunts that took place in that locality. We know the locality. The vicinity of the village of Fenelon Falls between Cameron and Sturgeon lakes was one of the Indian hunting grounds. At all events Balsam lake where the late George Laidlaw had established his home and where his son who saw service in South Africa now resides was one of the camping places of Champlain and I want to direct the right hon. First Minister's attention to the fact. We do not want a $5,000 monument erected here but we will be very much pleased to see something to commemorate the adventures of Champlain in that locality erected in the county of Victoria.
Sir WILFRID T, A FRIER. I am most delighted to hear the sentiments expressed by my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes). We will be very happy to do for Ontario what we have been able to do for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. There was a celebration this year at Annapolis of the 300th anniversary, of the landing of De Monts at Annapolis Royal. This Historical Society of Nova Scotia asked the government to contribute a certain amount towards the erection of a monument to Champlain. This appropriation which we ask parliament to vote has been asked for by the Historical Society of New Brunswick. Parliament has responded very cheerfully to that request and no doubt if any similar organization from Ontario were to send us a similar request it would meet with the same response. The city of St. John wants to put up a better monument than a monument which could be erected for $5,000. We give $5,000 and the city are to contribute an additional sum towards this monument. We shall be guided by the requests which are made upon us but we shall take into consideration any request that is made to us, and if it so happens that we are still in charge of af-Mr. SAM HUGHES.
fairs we will have still more pleasure in doing so.
Mr. GOL'RLEY. It is very proper that the erection of monuments to commer-morate the achievements of the early French explorers should be started in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. De Monts, the first European subject to land on this continent made his first landing at Annapolis Royal in 1604. Champlain a short time afterwards landed at St. John. Therefore it is very proper, chronologically considered, that these monuments should be first erected in the places which these men made historic by their first association with them. Afterward, I have no doubt Ontario will have the right to follow the maritime provinces and I will be very glad to join in any movement to that end. I was glad to hear my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughesl read that history which I am rather familiar with. I said some years ago in this. House : that Champlain and Cartier, the great early French explorers, had a better knowledge of Canada and its trade routes and its strong commercial position on this continent, than any men in Canada since, with all our education.
Is this going to be a contribution ?

speechtext:
