Valleyfield public buildings, $30,000.
What is the total cost to be ?
The total estimated cost is $55,000. The total expenditure has been $25,000 and this vote will complete.
Does it include the land V
Yes, everything.
It is a combined building for post office, &c.

Yes ; this is to complete the contract.
Seven Islands-wharfs, $60,000.
I handed my hon. friend the contract in this matter.
Who had the contract from the private parties to build this pier?
Connolly of Quebec.
Why did not the government allow Connolly to go on with the work for the company, in view of the statement made last year by the minister.

The engineer says that the department looked very carefully into the matter and that the transfer was in the public interest. The hon. gentleman has read the contract and he knows that , tshte material and labour will have to be

certified by the chief engineer before any payment is made.
Does this company buy the material from themselves ?

Wherever they get it cheapest; the price of the timber has to be certified by the engineer and there is to be a certified sworn copy of the number of men and the wages and in addition we have a resident engineer.

How is the price of the lumber to be determined V We were told yesterday it would be folly to ask for tenders to do this work because this company was in such a position of superiority that they might charge any price they liked. Are they to be allowed to put in any price they like now ?
I do not think so. Our engineer has a thorough knowledge of the price of timber all over.

It is not clear to me why the company were not allowed to go on and do the work themselves, and why the government assumed the responsibility of it when it was being done by a private corporation. This corporation had received pulp concessions and water privileges, and in order to make these valuable they had to erect deep water piers and they let a contract for that purpose, as I understand from the minister. When the work was pretty well under way the government stepped in and in a paternal spirit took it oft' their hands and allowed them $34,000 for the work done, and $21,000 for the material on hand, and then authorized them to go on and complete the work. Why did the government interfere ?

The reason the government, after acquiring the wharf, did not allow the contractors to continue the work was that there was really no plan that would satisfy the engineers of the department. Plans were prepared by the department, and it was on these plans that the work was proceeded with.
It has not been made clear why the government interfered and took over the work.
It was' on the opinion of the chief engineer. The bon. gentleman knows that the minister has practically to follow his technical officer.
Have you the report of the engineer there ?
Yes.
We are rather interested to find out how the engineer happened to go there. Who sent" him there ?
It is not possible for the chief engineer to visit every place where work is being carried on.

Did the engineers drift in there by accident, and say : We ought to take this work over and extend it, and do it on a more elaborate scale ; we will give $34,000 to the contractor for the work done and $21,000 for the material ; we will take it from the contractor, and then hand it back to him and tell him to go on and complete the work ; and he will send us a statement of the materials supplied to him at a certain price and the amount paid in wages ; and if the engineer certifies to it, we will pay you ? Is that the Whole plan ?

If the hon. gentleman looks at the papers, he will see that it was not done in that way at all. He will find, in addition to the certificate of our engineer, a certificate attached of Messrs. Ross and Holgate, both in regard to the amount of work done by the contractor and the amount of material on hand.
Is Mr. Holgate the company's engineer ?
Yes.

The minister has not yet given us any reason for taking this work over. He has given us a description of the course followed in getting a report from the government engineer and also from the engineers of the company ; but what the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) is anxious to know is why the government wanted to take this property over at a time when the company were building the work themselves, and had spent $55,000 or $56,000 upon it. That is the point the hon. member for Toronto is endeavouring to make, and the minister does not seem to catch the point.

I did not understand the hon. member for Toronto to make that point. The reason for it is this. There is an item in the estimates for a pier at this place. It was explained last night very fully by the hon. Minister of Justice that this is the only harbour on the north shore of the St. Lawrence for a very long distance. It was felt by the department that the government should own and control the wharf at such an important harbour of refuge ; and when the government found that this company had started the wharf, they felt that they -should, in the interest of the country, take it over from the company instead of building a new one, and the interest of the public was carefully guarded in the method pursued.
Is this wharf to be built exactly where the old wharf was ?
Yes.
What kind of timber will you use in the wharf ?
Mostly southern pine for the face timber.
Is that pine grown in the j southern states or at the Seven Islands ?
I understand from the term ' southern pine ' that it is grown in the south.

Sometimes it is called southern pine, though it never grew in the south.
Mx\ HYMAN. It is certified by two engineers that it is southern pine, and by southern pine the department understands pine that has grown in the south.
Are you aware that is the fact ?
I take that from the engineers. I am not aware of the fact.
There is another ' nigger in the fence ' there.

The government allowed this Seven Islands bay to remain for a number of years without providing a harbour of refuge there. Now they are engaged in carrying on this work. No doubt their attention was called to it by some request either from parties interested in shipping or parties interested in the business. Is there anything on file in the department to show how the government discovered the necessity for this wharf ?
I am informed by the engineer that it is purely the act of the government, just as I explained before.

Would it be the act of the government without somebody drawing their attention to the necessity for a wharf 7 Is the government sending engineers all around the country to hunt up places where there ought to be wharfs, without any applications being made for them, either from the shipping interests or the public in general ? We are told that this is the only harbour of refuge on that shore, but that has been told us in support of several different items, and that plea is pretty well worn threadbare. It is about time that some better excuse was offered. There might be some excuse if there was any population in that place ; but so far as we know, it has neither population or commerce to any extent worth mentioning and is comparatively speaking a wilderness. But simply because two or three enterprising individuals, finding that there were good timber limits and water-powers in that region, applied to the province of Quebec and got hold of these timber limits and water-powers and started business, and simply because, after they had begun building a wharf which was absolutely necessary to them in the prosecution of their industry, these people found it would be much more advantageous to them to have that work done as a public work, we find this government stepping in and taking the expense off their hands and on the plea of serving the public interest build-Mr. HYMAN.	,
ing a wharf for this particular firm. That is really what this expenditure amounts to. This company had done work on that wharf to the extent of some $34,000 and had lumber and other material there, estimated to be worth some $21,000, and the government repay them this expenditure, and then tell them to go on and complete the job and we will recoup you for what it may cost. There is not the slightest evidence that there has been any request from any shipping or commercial interests for this work except from the private company I have referred to. A more wanton piece of extravagance, to use a mild term, could scarcely be exhibited even by this business and reform government.

I said last night that the government appear to be overflowing with love for these Messrs. Clarke, and I am still of that opinion. This place, called the Seven Islands, has been inhabited for no less than 200 years by fishermen and mariners, who navigate in small boats that draw from four to six feet of water, and who had all the accommodation they needed from the little wharf that was built there.. During all this time, while these poor fishermen and mariners were the sole inhabitants of that region, no government thought it worth while to spend any money on public improvements on behalf of these people. But no sooner did the Messrs. Clarke secure lumber limits and water-power in that district and start a big business, than this government steps in and takes the wharf, which these people had begun to build, off their hands and are now about to complete it at a great expense to the country. This of course will be eminently satisfactory to the Messrs. Clarke, who own the whole country for several miles up the river and several miles back. They own that country absolutely. Under the charter given them a couple of years ago, no one has the right to build a store there or a hotel or start a place of commerce of any kind. Mr. Clarke owns everything, and yet this paternal government is going to build a wharf especially for him and his associates. Looking at it in any light you please, it appears to me the height of absurdity that any government should have so much love for some men and so very little for others. These poor fishermen and mariners who were in that place long before the Clarkes, were just as much entitled to government favours, but they never got anything. And this government, which claims to be the protector of the people, which claims to carry the whole country on its hands, which, we are told, was going to give a great example of reform, never dreamt of doing anything for the poor people in that locality. But no sooner did the Clarkes take possession of it, than these ministers are ready to kneel down and pray for them.

As I understand from the records, this work was being proceeded with by the company which owns the limits before the vote of last year was asked for. If the government knew anything about the matter, they must have known that the company was then constructing a pier of its own for its own purposes. The House was not put in possession then of anv of the information we have to-night, although if the government engineer had been down there and had made a report on the necessity of constructing a pier for the purpose of establishing a harbour of refuge, he would certainly not have failed to mention all the facts. I have not yet been able to satisfy myself that there was any justification for the interference of the government in this work. The privileges which this company had obtained had to be exploited, and in order to exploit them the company had to build a wharf, and were doing it when the appropriation was voted by parliament last year. The next thing we find is that the work which was being performed by this company has been taken over by the government, and the government has undertaken to pay the company some $50,000 to $00,000 for work done and material in hand. That certainly is not a very satisfactory proposition to my mind.

It would appear from these papers that months before the government asked for a vote of $25,000 last year, this work was under way. It was begun by the company in April, 1903, and continued until November. The sum of $34,000 had been expended by the company at the time the government asked parliament for a vote for the purpose of erecting a wharf of its own. It now appears that the purpose was to purchase the work which the company had begun. And we find that the government had undertaken to do this without any interested party, unless it be this company interested, asking that it be done. The public of Canada has not asked for this work. The shipping interests have not approached the government in order to have the sum of $25,000 put in the estimates to pay for the work which was being constructed by private parties. But in the course of the early months of 1904, the government bound itself to pay the company for the portion of the work already constructed, the sum of $34,433.75, and the agreement goes on to provide :
That over and above the said sum, for all the materials, inoiuding pine, spruce, iron, &c., which have already been delivered on the site and for the purpose of the contemplated works, the government hind itself to pay the said company, once for all a further sum of $21,485.34, it being clearly understood and agreed that all such materials are to he used in the carrying out of the construction of the balance of the works contemplated.

9.	As to the labour the said company shall produce pay-rolls duly receipted and containing a certificate signed in the manner determined in the preceding clause to the effect that the labour mentioned in such pay-rolls has been actually and necessarily performed and paid for in connection with the carrying out of the said balance of the works.
And this is the plan on which the government generously came to the relief of this company. They took over work for $10,000 more than parliament had justified the government in spending, and also covenanted to pay them $22,000 for material which the government had not authorized them to pay at all, and then bound themselves to go on and spend nearly $100,000, and perhaps more
Not more.
Probably more, because there is no limit.
I am sure the hon. member (Mr. Bell) does not wish to be unfair. He knows very well that there is a limit. I have told him that there were plans and specifications, and they are referred to.
If, under the operation of this peculiar contract the government vote is exhausted, the minister has prudently made provision
The hon. gentleman knows that the vote as taken is mentioned. Last year I think the minister told the House that it would require $60,000.
But it is evident that the minister contemplated that the company would spend more than the vote, because he has put in this provision.
Because the plans might lie changed.

He has put in this provision :
10.	Should the amount now voted by parliament and applicable towards payment lor the works hereby contracted lor be at any time expended previous'to the completion ol the said works, the contractor shall not be entitled to any payment lor work done beyond the amount voted and applicable as aforesaid until the necessary lunds shall have been voted by parliament in that behalf.
We only had $25,000 at that time and so that seemed a necessary provision.
Quite an amount for an ordinary wharf-$25,000. We would be glad of half of it in our section.

This is clearly one of the most extraordinary transactions that have come before the notice of this House. In discussing this matter last night attention was called to the fact that no tenders were called for this work. The reason advanced by the minister for this course was that no person would be in a position to tender except the company interested, because material could be supplied by them to better advantage than by any one else. Now, I find in the specification of timber as submitted by the government engineer that the greater part of that timber is southern pine, valued at $28 per thousand.
It is $27 per thousand is it not ?

Perhaps it is $27 or $28 per thousand. Certainly, any other company as well as one engaged in the production of pulp on the St. Margaret river would be in as good a position to procure southern pine as they would. So, there is nothing whatever to justify the government in spending $85,000-supposing it be no more -in violation of the Act that requires that works of this kind should be carried out by tender and contract. That Act provides as follows:
The minister shall invite tenders by public advertisement tor the execution of all works, except in cases of pressing emergency in which delay would he injurious to the public interest, or in which, from the nature of the work, it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department-
This is not by officers of the department.
Certainly it is.
I understood that the only officer there was a resident engineer.
All those engaged in the work under that clause are officers and servants of the government while engaged on the work.

In that case, the North Shore Power and Pulp Company is an officer of the government, because that is the party doing the work.
-or in cases where the estimated cost is less than $5,000.
Regarded from every point of view, there is really nothing that has been said to this House that justifies this transaction. The idea of this being built as a harbour of refuge is one that escaped the attention of the government! for seven years. (Only now, when certain parties want to build it do they make the discovery that it is necessary to make these important works. The reason given for not publicly calling for tenders is quite inadequate and offers no justification for adopting this course. There was no question of emergency, and there is nothing to show that it is more in the interest of the government to build this without tender than in the case of any other contract in which the government are engaged. If the government can take refuge under that section to justify the carrying out of this work in the way they are doing it practically they have set aside any other obligation resting upon them to perform any part of the public works of this country by tender and contract. If this is to be the interpretation placed upon the section by the minister, the whole system that has been looked upon as, in a certain measure, a security to the people of the country is wiped out. Because, there is no public work going on in Canada for which such justification c.vild not be found if 1be go [DOT] ernment chose to do the work in the manner in which they are doing it here-by buying the materials and supplying the labour.
I suppose the engineer has given to the minister the height, length and width of the wharf, and how many thousand feet of lumber and timber will be used in the contraction ?

He made plans of the wharf, and, of course, those plans give all the measurements.
Mr- COCHRANE. The minister tells us that there were plans and specifications, and, as I understand, work was done under them. But now a new plan has been adopted. How are the engineers going to apply the work done under the old plan to the lines of the new ?
The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has the report which explains the matter.
Are these all the documents connected with the matter that are on file in the department 1

All the documents under which this contract is made. I asked for all

the documents and these are all that were laid before me.

This item was discussed on the 9tli October last year. The statement made by the Minister of Public Works was a very brief one. He said :
This is to make provision for the construction of a deep water pier on the west side of Bay of Seven Islands. The pier will run out in a northerly direction, nearly at right angles to the shore, and it will have a total length of 1,325 feet, reaching a depth of 48 feet at low water spring tide. The estimated cost is $65,000. The reason for the work is that there is a most important development going on at that place, and there are now large pulp mills in that district which was up to a year or so ago almost unknown.
That statement was made on October 9. That statement bears evidence that the department had sent an engineer down there, and that the engineer had made a survey
The hon. gentleman can make any deductions he pleases ; as a matter of fact an engineer had not been sent down at that time.

The hon. gentleman can then explain the meaning of the language which his colleague used in asking the committee twelve months ago for this appropriation. He gave particulars as to the location of the dock ; he told us in what position it was to be located ; he told us how it would run out; he told us it would be at right angles to the shore running out in a northerly direction ; he told us it would have a total length of 1,354 feet and that it would have a depth of forty-eight feet at low water spring tide. The estimated cost was $65,000. We have surely the right to infer, if any value is to be placed on the statement made to the committee last October by the Minister of Public Works, that he had data upon which he made that statement and gave those particulars. If there had not been an engineer down there then we cannot attach much value to the statement. If the department had not sent an officer to make a survey of the harbour, to decide on the best site for the pier, of what dimensions it should be, and how it should run, if this statement of the minister is all to be cast aside, then I cannot say much more about it. The House or any person reading his statement would certainly conclude that the minister was speaking on the authority of some information given to him by an engineer of his department. How did he know the length the pier would be, or what it would cost ? Have we a right to infer that the minister imagined these things, or that he had some officer in his department who advised him as to what the probable cost would be ? How could he ascertain what the cost would be if he did not know the dimensions of the pier and the probable cost of material down there ?
Those remarks of the minister were made on October 9. Parliament prorogued about October 24, and this correspondence commenced, so far as the papers brought down show, on November 23. The first letter is dated from Quebec less than a month after prorogation, and six weeks after the statement of the minister. It is as follows :

Sir,-During the last session of parliament the sum of $25,000 was granted towards the construction of a breakwater in the harbour of Seven Islands, county of Saguenay, Quebec. The building of a breakwater was, however, commenced by the North Shore Power, Railway and Navigation Company, under contract with Mr. Michael Connolly, the amount expended by the company to date being, according to the inclosed letter from Mr. Thomas Mr. CLARKE.
Meaney, secretary-treasurer of the company, $34,433.95. The contract prices were fixed by the company after calling for tenders from a number of reliable contractors. None of the tenders being found satisfactory, an agreement was entered into with Mr. Connolly to perform the work at prices lower than those of any tender received, and I am satisfied that the prices affixed to the different quantities of work already performed are fair and reasonable. I therefore believe it would be in the interest of the department to purchase from the company for the amount of the expenditure incurred to date, the portion of the work which they have already built, and to continue the breakwater to completion on the site adopted by them, which is the one they have deemed best suitable for the purpose it was intended to serve.
The company are the owners of the site of, and the approach to, the work commenced by them. It would therefore be necessary, should the department take over the work, for the company to vest in the Crown the deep water lot upon which the wharf is to be built, as well as all the land required for freight' sheds, &c., and the road across the property, for the public use.
With the plans at my disposal I am unable to locate and properly describe the land required for the road and storage accommodation, and it is impossible at this season of the year to send an engineer to make the necessary survey. This, however, if an agreement is entered into with the company, could be done as early as possible next spring, and before the actual work of construction was commenced. I have not at my disposal the necessary plans with soundings on the site of the proposed work, and I will cause contract plans and specifications to be prepared as soon as I am advised that the work already performed by the company has been vested in the crown, and that the company have agreed to give all the land required for the public use of the wharf when completed.

This is all the correspondence in this bunch except some one or two typewritten statements as to quantities of timber, southern pine, &c. It was pointed out by the Minister of Justice last year that this work ought to be done. In the course of the speech which he made recommending the appropriation of |25,000, he said :
It is of the greatest importance to the navigation of the St. Lawrence that there should be a port in the Bay of Seven Islands, which would be a place of refuge for the vessels, and where they could be repaired. It would be in the public interest to have a wrecking plant and a dry-dock there. It is really more central than Quebec, where there is a wrecking plant now. When a vessel gets aground, it is of the utmost importance that she should be taken off at the earliest possible moment, so as to be saved the consequences of the terrible battering she would get if a storm came on. If a vessel happens to he stranded and is allowed to remain on the rocks for a week, and one of those terrific storms which we have down there comes on, she will, as the saying is, practically pound the bottom out of herself. This place is not in my constituency, but is in the constituency of my 1:on. friend '(Mr. Girard) ; but it is the only point on the lower St. Lawrence where there is a harbour, and it is important that we should have at that central point conveniences for enabling us to go to the help of vessels which may be wrecked in the locality. This work is not for the benefit of one firm only. All those American firms which come in there for the purpose of exploiting our spruce limits will use this port as a port of shipment. How can you ship pulp from the lower St. Lawrence if you cannot get vessels into a harbour whence it can be shipped ?
Just a few weeks after that statement was made as to the necessity of this work we find the government in negotiation to acquire a property about which the engineer practically knew nothing, because he makes no certificate as far as I can see here. He says that it is impossible to send an engineer down at that season of the year. He accepts a work constructed by a private company on its own property. He accepts the statement of the secretary treasurer of the company accompanied by the certificate of the company's engineers, and upon the strength of that he recommends, and the government accept the recommendation, that this pier at Seven Islands, and which was being constructed by this private company in its own interest, should be taken over at the company's price. The government also assume the responsibility for the completion of the
work and pay for all the work and materials which the company have done or supplied and the government's engineer certifies to the account. If this is a satisfactory way of doing business, why then I do not think I should occupy any more of the time of the committee. It seems to me to be a most unbusiness like proposition. It seems to me that the committee was not placed in possession of all the information which it had a right to expect from the hon. minister when he asked for this vote last year. There has been no reason advanced yet why the government should have taken this work over and made the contract which it has made with this company. I enter my protest as one member of the committee against this method of doing business because I think it is not in the public interest that business should be done in this way. The hon. gentleman may have all these letters and documents now.
Would the hon. min-itser please answer that question ?
I have endeavoured to explain the item several times.	,
The hon. gentleman did not explain the question I put to him.
What was the question ?
I thought the hon. minister was paying some attention to what I was saying.
It is pretty hard to remember the question after the long oration we have had from the hon member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke.)

The question was if the wharf was partly built in accordance with one specification how the government could adopt a new specification and work it out. This is an extraordinary position to take and I think the hon. acting minister will see how fallacious his statement is when he pretends to shelter himself behind the wording of the statute. I know that when he thinks the matter over he will see that the statute was never intended to cover a case like this. I am here to tell the acting minister that if he has no alternative, but to accept the recommendation of his engineer he had better get out of the business. The hon. minister has power to either accept or reject the recommendation of his engineer. I never knew that the department was run by the engineer. I knew it would be pretty hard for the minister to adopt every recommendation of the engineer, but I never knew that the minister was compelled to accept every recommendation that the engineer made. If that is the stand that the minister takes he is in a very absurd position. If a private individual got money in the same way that the hon. Minister of Public Works got money from this committee last year he would soon be put behind the penitentiary bars. He got the money under false pre-

teDses. He asked for money to commence a work when it was already commenced, and it cost the country somewhere about $34,000 to pay for the work that had already been done. I think it is an absurd proposition to say that if they change their minds in reference to a work they cannot call for new tenders. They had to change their plans and specifications. I would like to ask the hon. minister what there was to hinder him from asking for public tenders for the work. The hon. minister will realize that he cannot shelter himself behind that clause of the statute because that clause of the statute was framed to meet a different situation. Should sudden emergency arise on a canal or public work the statute was designed to enable the government to employ the men on the canal or public work in finishing up the work. It is absurd to say that because these men are hired by the government they are officials of the government. It is absurd to say that the labouring men employed on this wharf are government officials. The engineer is a government official, but outside of that they are not government officials; they are hired men. We all know, from what has transpired here, that it costs about twenty-five per cent more for the government to do work by day's labour than by contract. If this work is necessary, I am prepared to vote the money, but I must be sure that it is in the best interests of the people of Canada, and that no private individual will be reaping a rich harvest out of the hard earnings of the people of this country.
I am sure that when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) sees his words in ' Hansard ' he will regret stating that the Minister of Public Works last year asked the House for money under false pretenses.
Yes.
There is not one tittle of evidence before this committee-
Would the minister tell me

Excuse me; I have the floor. There is not one tittle of evidence before this House which would show that in October last, T*hen the minister asked for this vote, he had any knowledge whatever of the fact of there being a wharf there that time.
Then how did his officer make a report ?

I am stating, in answer to the charge made, that when the minister asked for this vote there is not a tittle of evidence to show that he knew there was a wharf in existence. He said it was proposed to build a wharf there ; he gave the cost at $65,000, and he pursued the usual course in initial votes in asking for a sum in the estimates sufficient to enable the
department to enter into a contract, but not enough to complete the work. It was decided afterwards that it would-be more in the public interest that the government should acquire the property that had already been constructed.
And the minister did not know it. When ignorance is bliss it is folly to be wise.

Very often, when a work has progressed to the extent of forty or even fifty per cent, if in the opinion of the engineer it is in the public interest to change the plans, the plans are changed without in any possible way interfering with the work already done. In this case there were certain changes made in the plans of the engineer, notwithstanding that there had been an expenditure of $34,000. It is quite true that a minister does not of necessity have to follow the reports made by his engineer, but he must be very largely guided by these reports. I do not say in all cases the minister is obliged to concur, but it is a very serious matter if he goes against his engineer's reports, and if I tried to justify such a thing in this House I have no doubt hon. gentlemen opposite would make a serious attack on me.
I referred to the engineer's recommendation.

His recommendation in writing and his report are practically the same thing. The engineer is a technical officer and it is a serious thing for the minister to override on a purely technical question, the report of an engineer who has been in the department for many years.
The minister has left his department in a worse hole than before he attempted a defence. I can tell him that when I see ' Hansard ' I will not be sorry for what I said.
I am sorry you won't.

You need not be sorry for me ; be sorry for yourself. You are responsible for the blunder you made in playing into the hands of a certain party that you think more of, it looks to me, than you do of the public funds of this country. What is the position of the minister after challenging me for my impertinent statement?
I never said that.
Let me speak now.
The hon. gentleman is quick enough to interrupt me-
Or otherwise.
If the company were constructing a work there and willing to spend their money on it, I cannot for the life of me see why the government should assume that work.
The vote was passed in October, 1903. There was no payment made to the company until after the report of the engineer of the 25th of June, 1904.
But the work was done.
The papers show that the work had been commenced by the company in 1903.

I can appeal to the hon. gentleman that if time has been taken up on this item, it is due to the paucity of the information which he gave to the committee When this matter came up yesterday. Theiv, is some cause for complaint that the full information to which the committee was entitled has not been laid before it ; because I maintain, with all respect for the hon. gentleman's officers, that the file of correspondence which has been laid on the table does not contain all the correspondence which took place between the persons from whom this wharf was purchased and the department. That is rather- an unfortunate state of affairs. The engineer did not recommend that the site of this company's dock should be accepted. He did not recommend that the proposition made to this committee by the Minister of Public Works last year Should be abandoned altogether. He does not say that the wharf which the government has taken over is on the same site and in the same location and is for the same purpose for which a vote of $25,000 was taken last year to commence the construction of a government pier. The engineer should not be held responsible for the action of the government. The engineer's report speaks for itself. The engineer is very prudent and very cautious in making his statement, and that statement was not made until almost a month after the secretary-treasurer of the company had sent a certificate to the minister of the value of the work done on the wharf and asked for a cheque for it. The statement of the engineer points out that this wharf or pier is on private property, and that before the
government can do anything in the matter the property will, of course, have to be deeded to the Crown. The engineer recommended further that the material for which the country is to pay, or has paid, $21,000 or $22,000, should be charged up to the contractor for the work at the same price that the government paid to the company. That, it seems to me, would imply that the engineer of the department desired that the remainder of the work should be done by contract. Will the hon. gentleman pass over the report or read that portion of it ?

At these prices, -which I deem fair and reasonable, the above mentioned materials would cost $21,485.34, and, as they are already delivered on the site of the work, a clause might be inserted in the specification to the effect that intending contractors would agree to take over these materials at the prices mentioned.

If the engineer knew what he was writing, and I suppose he did, he intended that tenders should be called for the completion of the work, because he recommended that if tenders were called for, the successful tenderer should be charged the same amount for the material on hand that the government had paid -the company for it. The transaction ail through is in a very unsatisfactory shape, and if we reach wrong conclusions in regard to it, it will be because we have not received all the information we are entitled to. I understand the peculiar difficulty the acting minister finds himself in, because this correspondence took place and this report was made prior to his assuming charge of the department ; but it was the duty of his officers to supply all this information, so that we might form an intelligent judgment upon the matter. I think it is a vicious principle for the government to ask parliament for a vote for a specific purpose, and then to ignore the intention of parliament, apply the money to another purpose, purchase private property, and do it all in the most careless and slipshod way. The hon. gentleman said this money was not to be paid over until June last. The contract was not completed until the 23rd of June, the date on which it was signed. Have the officers of the department obtained any information as to whether the storms of last fall and winter damaged the work that was constructed ?
We have no information as to any damage having been done to the work.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I think the opposition have a perfect right to object to this item. Last year -the government prepared their estimates in Council, laid them before parliament and asked for $25,000, and the minister, when asked by this side of the House what that was for, stated that it was for the purpose of erecting a wharf, giving the name of the place, the kind of wharf that

was to be constructed, the necessity for it, its dimensions, and everything else connected with it. The opposition accepted the minister's statement that it was a work of necessity and in the interest of the country, and supposed that the government would proceed with the work as all public works are carried on, by first getting a report from their engineer and then calling for tenders. But what do we find to-day ? If there is any truth in the statement which I have in my hand, and which I am going to read, the government must issue a commission anil have this matter investigated. A party who has been on the ground writes this letter :
Dear Sir,-I regret to say that conditions were not favourable to take a photograph of the work I saw going on at ' Clarke's City,' in the bay of Seven Islands, for I would dearly like to show the people of this country how they are being ' flim-flammed ' and their money squandered in aiding the schemes o'f unscrupulous adventurers, from across the border, for a consideration, enlist the active support of one of the members of this ' business ' government.
In this instance I refer to the operations of the company known as the North Shore Power, Railway and Navigation Company, * a body corporate and politic, with head office in New York, though I think they have an office in Quebec, for which, like Gaynor & Green, the firm of the Hon. (?) Charley Fitzpatrick is counsel, &c. Anyway, it was that hon. gentleman, who got this company its charter, and has ever since watched over it with fatherly care.
Some two years ago, this aggregation of New York adventurers, through the efforts of Fitzpatrick's firm, of which Mr. Parent, premier of Quebec, is a member, secured a tract of timber and pulpwood lands, situated on the River St. Marguerite, about three hundred miles below Quebec. After this, they purchased, for a nominal sum, the water power of the River St. Marguerite, and began to make such improvements as seemed necessary for the manufacture of pulp. For this purpose, it was necessary to have an outlet on Seven Islands bay, so a railroad about nine or ten miles long running from the first falls of the Ste. Marguerite to Seven Islands bay was projected-but I understand/ It is fiot yet finished-ail the rolling stock of which has been allowed in free of duty ; but this is not the worst 'feature, from a public standpoint, of the ' encouragement ' that has been extended to this J infant industry.' A deep water terminus was necessary, so this company set to work to build a wharf, by extending out in the bay, a rock embankment, from the excavations along the line of railway to a distance of about eight hundred feet, or to a depth of about ten or twelve feet of water, where the first section o'f a timber wharf about two hundred feet long and thirty wide was placed, and filled up to low water with stone from the excavation. This much was accomplished last year ; but towards the close of the season, the North Shore Power, Railway and Navigation Company discovered that they had undertaken an expensive experiment, and ways and means were discussed to induce the government to undertake the expense of pro-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
viding this company with the wharf and terminal facilities for their own business ; and strange as it may seem, the Department of Public Works have taken over, and paid for all the work and material supplied by this company on account of the terminal facilities required for its own use. There is not a habitation or living man residing within miles of this wharf, and no person will ever use it, but this pulp proposition (if it ever is finished.)
I understand this scheme was worked last year by the Hon. ' Charley ' Fitzpatrick, who induced the Minister of Public Works to put an item in the estimates ($25,000) for a wharf at Seven Islands. This passed the House all right, for Seven Islands is an old Hudson Bay post, and still something of a trading station with the Indians ; but is fully nine miles across the bay from Clarke City, where the wharf is being built. Then during the present session of parliament, another appropriation o'f $60,000 has been asked, making in all so far $85,000 to aid a scheme that is no earthly use to any one outside the aggregation comprising this pulp syndicate, Fitzpatrick, Girard et al ; but presumably some of this money will be laid aside to help Girard, M.P., for the district, and the Hon. Charley through the next election.
I am credibly informed that the North Shore Power, Railway and Navigation Company is building this wharf by days' labour, and furnishing the material at abnormally big prices, and the Department of Public Works is paying the bills monthly.
No wonder Fitzpatrick et al were desirous of getting rid of the Auditor General.
Why should these bills be paid ? Even if the work were required for the general good of Canada, the Public Works Department, has no authority to assume the expense of such a job without letting the work by public tender. It is easy for such cattle to find money to debauch the electorate, if they are allowed to go on in this manner.
Ask for a royal commission to investigate the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Signed by whom ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: By a gentleman who, if given the commission, will produce evidence to substantiate every word that is in that paper. If these are the facts, it is the duty of the government to name a commission and see whether these statements are correct or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman pass me over the paper ? I find there is no signature to this document which the hon. gentleman has read. Kindly give us the name.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman name a commission ?
Name.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Either one of two things. The hon. gentleman has read a document which

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Which was placed in my hands by a responsible party, who, he says, will verify every statement it contains.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said that It was signed by a responsible party.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I did not say it was
signed, but that it was placed in my hands by a responsible party.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will he give the name of the responsible party or, in the alternative, make himself responsible for the truth of those statements, and they will be met very quickly.

There is another alternative. These statements just read are alleged to be correct. We have no knowledge whether they are correct or not. They were read before the Minister of Justice, who is one of the parties named, and the reading of these statements affords him an opportunity of either denying or explaining them or attaching what weight to them be thinks fit. They are made in such a way that he can set this House right. If any members of this House are improperly informed or wrongfully informed, or if the *allegations are not correct, the opportunity is given him of setting the House right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I must confess that I am surprised that my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) for whom, as he knows, I have very great regard, would take the responsibility of saying here that an anonymous document of this sort must be answered in this House. The document has been read in the House, and I ask now that it be laid on the table to form part of the records so that we may know with what we are dealing. Independent altogether of the statement appearing in ' Hansard ' which gives it some weight, in view of the fact that it was read by the chief whip of the [DOT]opposition, I want this document to be in the custody of the House because I know something of this document and I know it did not reach the chief whip of the opposition direct but came to him through another channel. In this paper, these gentlemen, the Clarke Company are said to be a firm of New York adventurers. Sir, there is not a member of that firm, so far as my recollection goes-and I am pretty certain that I am *correct-who is not a Canadian. The members of the firm are the Clarke Brothers of Toronto, who also do business in New York, but who have remained British subjects. They never changed their allegiance. It is said here that this firm acquired these timber limits by-I do not know exactly what process described, but evidently the' writer of this paper suggests that they were acquired by some improper method. Sir, they were acquired by that firm at public auction after competition. No public timber limits can be sold in the province of Quebec except at public auction. That is provided by statute. With respect to the water-powers, I do not know anything about
the way they were acquired. Nor do I know anything about the incorporation of the company. I left my law firm in 1896, and have never been actively engaged in the management of it since then. I know absolutely nothing of what was done and am absouteJy unconnected with the management of my firm in any way, shape or form, except that nay name appears in it. In view of these facts and in view of the fact that this production is anonymous-
Disreputable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is, to say the least, unfair to make it the basis of an attack upon me. I do not know of anything I have done at any time since I have been connected with the House which would justify any gentleman in assuming, on the strength of an anonymous letter, that I would for a consideration-for that is what is stated-commit this House to an improper vote. All I know is that-as I stated last year and repeat now-this coast, extending from Tadousac to the entrance of the Straits of Belle Isle, a distance of' 600 odd miles, with a population of over 10,000, should have some facilities, and there is not a public wharf in the whole of that locality except at this point. As to whether or not the bargain was a provident or an improvident one, that is something which hon. gentlemen can judge for themselves. At all events I had absolutely nothing to do with the drawing of the contract. I never saw it until I read it to-night. I never saw anything of the correspondence exchanged until this moment, and I fail to understand what is the reason of this personal attack. It seems to me we can discuss matters of this sort without having recourse to such methods.
Is that all the explanation the minister has to give ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What further explanation do you require ?

I think the minister will be fair enough to admit that we are doing him an act of great kindness and justice when we bring to his attention the rumours which he alleges are entirely false, and which would create an erroneous impression if not explained by himself or some one else who knew the situation and the circumstances and could put the matter right. But when we give him this opportunity, he thinks we are doing him an act of unkindness. The hon. minister says I took the responsibility of that article.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not say that the hon. gentleman did. I said I was sure that the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) would not do it.
No, I would not, but since it is there, let me point out what is likely to be the public impres sion created by
it. The Minister of Justice, who is a member of the firm of Fitzpatrick, Parent and- what is the name V

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are five or six names in it.

Mr. Parent is the .premier of the province of Quebec and has under his control practically, or that of his government, the disposal of the timber lands and the water-powers in that province. The Minister of Justice lias given us a piece of valuable information, to my mind, and that is that the timber lands are sold by public auction. That being the case, we must assume that the gentlemen who purchased these limits, purchased them at tneir value in the market. So that there could be nothing wrong about that transaction whatever firm bought the limits. But the impression would have been left on the public mind, without such explanation, that in some way or other the premier of the province of Quebec, who is a partner of the Minister of Justice, had secured for this firm valuable timber limits and water-powers. There is no information as to it being secured properly or otherwise ; it is secured. There is no insinuation, so far as I know that any of the parties have individually profited.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is aware that, under the law of our province, there can be no sale of timber lands by the province except by public auction.

That is an illustration of what I have just said-that this gives the Minister of Justice an opportunity to make an explanation which the world at large does not know, and which puts a very different face upon the matter. With that explanation, it is clear that the firm could not have obtained the limit for less than it is worth. I do not know that any one has insinuated or would insinuate, after hearing this read together with the explanation of the minister, that either Mr. Parent or Mr. Fitzpatrick profited by this.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is insinuated that I got it for political purposes.

But, after this firm becomes possessed of the timber and waterpower through one member of the legal firm, another member of the same legal firm, who happens to be in the Dominion government advocates the building of a wharf there, and secures-or, if he does not secure it, at least there is secured through the Minister of Public Works-an item in the estimates for the building of that wharf. And, if the allegations be true that there is no settlement there and no commerce to be provided for, there would be no need for a wharf except to improve the facilities for this corporation. There is another eorpora-Mr. SPROULE.
tion there of which I happen to know in Ontario as a respectable firm. I say nothing against the firm of Clarke Brothers, because 1 know nothing about them. But we cannot suppose but that people will draw their own inferences from the facts that are placed before them. The fact that the Minister of Justice happens to be a member of the law firm that got the land and water-powers for this concern, and, immediately after; the Dominion government, of which he is a member, buy a. portion of the wharf that this lumber firm are building and add money to build a wharf which, according to the allegations made can be of no use except to further the interest of these parties ; and this is done upon an engineer's report which does not show that he has measured or verified in any way the quantity of work taken over but simply says that he believes the estimate of the timber is reasonable ; and on the strength of this the money is paid. The Minister of Public Works says that he knew nothing about the existence of a wharf there or of one being built. But the Minister of Justice had already told him by his statement in this House, which was as follows :
I know something of the bay of Seven Islands and this wharf partly built by a private company.
This statement was made when this item was under discussion. Yet, the Minister of Public Works says there is not a word to justify the statement that the Department of Public Works knew that there was such a work under construction, and there is no reason to insinuate that he knew that anything was being done except to begin de novo a wharf undertaken for philanthropic purposes or to facilitate the commerce of that region. We are told that there is no wharf for a great distance along that coast, and that these waters are considered the graveyard of the St. Lawrence. That would be a strong argument in favour of building a harbour of refuge. I felt like asking how many wrecks had taken place in these waters within the last twenty or thirty years. Because, if it could be shown that many wrecks had taken place, that would be an exceedingly strong argument in favour of a harbour of refuge. If, in addition, it had been shown that the navigators of those waters had applied to the gov-vernment for a harbour of refuge, I would say that that also was a strong argument in favour of it. But we endeavoured to get that information from the acting Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman) and also from the Minister of Public Works himself (Mr. Sutherland), but we got no information at all along that line. So, we have the right to assume that there was no demand and no application from the shipping interests of that section for a wharf. Taking all these things into consideration, we had just grounds for the assertion that this wharf

was built in the interest of this one concern and of this one concern alone. I am far from saying that even then it would not he justified, for, when people build up a great industry and give employment to labour, they are entitled to consideration, and they have their claims to be furnished with facilities, as well as people in any other part of the Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose that document will be placed on file in the House ? I request that it be placed on file.

There would be no object in doing otherwise. It was for the purpose of bringing out the information that it was brought forward. And my own suggestion regarding 'it was to have the name of the Minister of Justice mentioned in a document of this kind and in connection with such rumours as were current means either that the rumour should not be circulated or else there must be something behind it, that we did not know. Now, I thought it would do the minister greater justice to read it in his presence and allow him to make such explanation as he thought fit to have such a rumour going around the world where he was in no position to defend himself by making such explanation as he could make here.
Was not this company incorporated by this parliament or was it the railway company ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not this company, but the railway company.

I remember the minister making the explanation about this very place. I would like to have the plans of this shore and the wharf laid on the table that we may see whether this is going to be a harbour of refuge or simply an accommodation for the pulp factory. If the government fairly make the excuse that it will be a harbour of refuge, that Will be something in favour of this vote. But, if it is merely for the accommodation of this one corporation, the item has to come out so fat as the opposition are concerned. I wish to point out to the minister that the sums involved in this work and in that of Grande V a lice for the benefit of two lumber companies on the River St. Lawrence where there is no settlement would open up a hundred miles of navigation in a country that is well settled in the county of Victoria and Haliburton, by connecting a number of lakes and thus give the people there access to the world. And yet, we cannot get a dollar for those works. But these lumber companies walk up and get for such works as this and the Grande Vallee wharf, sums that are almost fabulous, the spending of which 'increases the value of their property, and the voting of which is so suspicious that a deal is charged by one of the government supporters in this House. And 2o4
the Minis ter of Justice knows it. I will not say he (Mr. Fitzpatrick) is a party to this matter. It is a Montreal district man who made the deal. And here is this other which looks like a deal, though we do not know the nature of it. If there is a harbour of refuge there well and good. But we ought to see the plans.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sam. Hughes) will not need to look at the plans. If he will look at the map, he will see that this is on the north shore of the St. Lawrence opposite the eastern extremity of the Island of Anticosti. This is a bay that is eleven m'iles wide and at least, eleven miles deep and practically land-locked. It affords perfect protection from the storms.

Where is this dock, in the bay V If so, what do you want a dock for in a harbour of refuge ? If you get into a land-locked bay what more do you want ? Why are not the plans of these things brought here '! We tried to get the plans for the Grande Vallde dock and I never saw them.

I am informed by the engineer, us the Minister of Justice has already sa'id, that this is a perfect harbour. This wharf is built there to close up part of the mouth of the harbour and thus reduce the width, making it a better shelter harbour, that is reduce the width of the mouth of the harbour and add material to make it a shelter harbour.
What was the depth of the harbour at their dock ? It is largely sailing vessels that are used there and these would want a wider entrance to come in.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is steamers altogether.
These sailing vessels would not want to make port through a narrow entrance.
The length of the dock 'is 1,100 feet.
Let us have a chart.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We will get Bayfield's chart.
Had we not better let this item stand ?
The matter has been fully discussed, and I do not think it should be discussed any longer.
I do not think it should pass at all.
Then move to strike it out.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Surely, in view of the statement which has been placed in my hands by a responsible party, who says he



lias been there, and in view of the fact that there is no contradiction of his statements, it is proved that the government came down last year and asked and obtained $25,000 to build a wharf, and at the same time, and six months before, the company were at work building a wharf. Now they come forward and ask another appropriation of $05,000. From the papers laid on the table of the House it is proved that no tenders were advertised for, that there was simply a bargain with these people who are to go ahead and complete it. If last year, when the committee was asked to vote $25,000 to commence this work, they had known all these circumstances, the ojiposition would have voted that this appropriation be struck out. I would, therefore, move that this item of $65,000 be struck out.
In listening to the reading of the certificate by the engineer I thought it was a very cautious one. Were there any subsequent surveys obtained by the department before they paid the money ?
The money was paid upon an account by the company upon the certificate of the two resident engineers and the chief engineer of the department.
Who were the two engineers ?
Mr. Tass& and Mr. Lamoureux.
Are they engineers of the department ?
They are both engineers of the department. One is district engineer and the other is resident engineer.
And they certify both as to quantity and price ?
Yes.
Are the certificates of these engineers there ?
They will be on the bill rendered by the company.
Have we that bill before us ?
What is here is simply a statement of the expenditure.
There is no certificate of any engineer there.
That will be filed.
There must be some more papers filed, because certainly that file is incomplete.
The bill rendered by the company would not form part of the papers in the possession of the department in any case.

If this embankment was constructed, as it has been said, by the company simply dumping in the harbour the Mr. TAYLOR.
stone from the excavations on the railway, and they were paid $1.25 a yard for that, the company must have reason to look on this as a fairly paternal government. That is a very fair rate of pay. We have not very full information in reference to this matter, and if the minister can assure us that he can give some further information, I think he should let the item stand until Monday.
The engineer informs me that there is really no further information that can be laid before the committee.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Surely there is some more correspondence that can be brought down. There must be the first application for a grant, and then an attempt should be made to reconcile the statement of the minister last year when he asked for the $25,000. I have produced here a statement that there is not a man within nine miles of this place. Surely, in the face of this statement, the government are not going to force it through.
At the mouth of what river is this pier being erected ?
The engineer informs me it is at Polnte Noir.

This committee are entitled to know if the government are in possession of any information or report from the engineer. We passed a vote of $25,000 last year to commence the construction of a pier for a specific purpose. The hon. gentleman's predecessor gave us particulars last year when he asked this vote of $25,000. It is not creditable to the department that we have to drag these statements out in order to get information to enable us to know what we are doing. The minister made specific statements as to the location of the dock, the length of the pier, depth of water, &c. He must have done that from some advice or report of his engineers. We are entitled to know why the engineer abandoned the location, why he accepted this new property, and if it will suit. He has made no statement to that effect in the documents which have been submitted to us.
I am informed by the engineer that the work which this vote is asked to complete will fulfil all the requirements that it was intended to fulfil when the vote of $25,000 was asked for.

I can only say that in so far as I am personally concerned that statement by the engineer will mitigate the conditions considerably, but we have a right to have some report from the engineer to justify this departure from the policy announced by the hon. Minister of Public Works last year.

I find that by the letter read that this wharf is not near the west side of the harbour of Seven Islands at all. It is said to be at the mouth of the St. Margaret river according to the letter

produced and it is shown by the chart in an air line to he seven and a half miles from the entrance to the river and up towards Quebec. I think you may assume that this is correct and the acting Minister of Public Works is ignorant of any knowledge as to where the wharf is to be.
Is the wharf marked on the chart ?	*

No, but I have the chart here showing that the St. Margaret river is seven miles west. The railway charter called for a road in the valley of the St. Margaret river. That is where the charter requires the railway to run, and here we find the St. Margaret river entering the St. Lawrence seven and a half miles above the harbour of Seven Islands. Seven Islands and the Hudson Bay post are away on the north side, and in an air-line across the isthmus it is eleven miles as stated in this report which has been read by my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor). I think that in face of all this the hon. minister should bring down some plans and not attempt to have this committee deceived by stating that this wharf is to be at the entrance of the Bay of Seven Islands. It is not according to the letter read, but is on the St. Margaret river and away up from the mouth of the harbour. Surely the hon. minister is not going to attempt to ask for a vote of this kind ?

I will ask the hon. gentleman not to use such intemperate language. I am making no attempt to deceive the committee at all. The hon. gentleman is making his statement upon an anonymous letter read to this committee by the hon. member for Leeds ; I am making my statement upon the statement of the engineer who assures me that the wharf is where I have stated it to be at the entrance to the harbour of Seven Islands. Surely I cannot be charged with misleading the committee under these circumstances.
Upon which side of the harbour is it, the east or the west ?
On the west side of the harbour.
How far is it from the village of Seven Islands, which I understand is on the east side of the harbour ?
The statement was made last year that the wharf is eight or nine miles from the village of Seven Islands.
Well, then, all we have to do' is to get the plans of the department.

The plans will not show the position of the wharf on the shore.
Mr. SaM. HUGHES. The plans will have to show where it is on the shore. They cannot show it in open water. I want to tell the hon. minister that if he says the har-254*
hour is on the west side then his statement a little while ago was absolutely unfounded. The hon. minister has made the statement based on the random and vague expressions of some of the officials of the department that this would narrow the entrance to the harbour.
The statement I made was that this would narrow the entrance of the harbour and I still maintain that is perfectly correct.

Well, then I will tell the hon. gentleman that his statement is absolutely wrong because the entrance to the harbour is on the southeast side of the bay and not on the west side of the bay, so that he had better look up his geography. I will send the plan over to him if he wants to see it.
Well, the hon. gentleman is making the statement.
No, he is not making that statement. He knows what he is talking about.
That is something new.

No, as hon. gentlemen know to their cost it is not something new. The hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Maepherson) will know it if he is not very careful. I will take him in hand some of these days and I will endeavour to civilize him a l'ittle.
He will take care of himself.
He will skip out the same as the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Bussell) did to-day.
The next time the hon. gentleman has anything to say to the member for Hants I hope he will say it when he is in the House and not when His back is turned.
Take it back.
I never take anything back. The statement of the hon minister is entirely wrong.
The statement is not entirely wrong. The statement is perfectly correct The wharf is built on the west side of the harbour and narrows the entrance of the harbour of Seven Islands.

We will take the statement here, although the engineer has not his plan, which is to the effect that the entrance to the harbour is on the southeast side of the bay and not on the west side. The hon. minister said that it was at the west side.
I said from the west side.

The minister did not say from the west side. He said at the west side. However, if he says he said from the west side I suppose I will have to accept his statement although I know what

lie said. He may have meant ' from ' but be said ' on.' I bad the chart in front of me at the time he made his statement. We find that the engineer has never visited the place and has no plan of it. He says that this railway runs along here. I want to see a plan of the harbour and I want to see where the railway line runs. If the railway is surveyed you can get the plans in the railway department. The plans must be registered, if so they must be in the Railway Department, and they will show where this line or railway runs, and also show its relationship to the bay, and we will be able to ascertain then when we see whether there is a dock there at all or not, nobody ever saw the dock.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: In view of the information laid before the committee to-night and in view of the statement which I have presented from a pally who says that he knows the facts to be correct as given, it is plain that we were humbugged last year in voting 825,000 on a statement made by the lion. Minister of Public Works which was not in accordance with the facts as represented to the committee to-night. We are now asked to vote $60,000 to carry on this job-it is nothing more or less than a job- which'is being perpetrated so that this amount of money can be given to a company of Americans. The lion. Minister of Jus-lice says that these gentlemen are British subjects although living in New York. Notwithstanding the fact that they are living in New York he says that these men have never become naturalized. Their business is carried on from New York and the hon. Minister of Justice has not contradicted the statement made in that letter.
What letter ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Well, that statement.
It is not a letter.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is a statement.
From Mr. Anonymous.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I Will ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) to ask the government to grant a commission and this gentleman will prove every statement made there.

I would expect from a member with the long experience of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) that he should know more than to stand up in this House and ask a commission on the strength of a statement made by a man who is either ashamed to sign it, or is too big a coward to sign it, or is a liar on the face of it. If this is the kind of statement the hon. gentleman expects a commission should be appointed on, I am afraid that his ideas of the dignity of this House are far below the mark.
Mr. TAYLOR, I have been in the House for twenty-two years, and I know that when the Liberals were in opposition dozens Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
and dozens of charges were made against, the Conservative party on the basis of such statements.
If that be so, I do not believe in it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
When information of this kind comes to the opposition, it is their duty to bring jt to the attention of the House no matter from what source it comes, and this communication is from a reliable source, "i lie hon. gentleman who placed that in my hand is reliable and he says that if lie is granted a commission he will establish every statement he makes and pay his side of the expense too. This is placed in my hands, as whip of the opposition, telling me it is my duty to bring it before the House, and I assume the duty and responsibility. If the statements there are true, this government ought to be swept from power at once. The Minister of Public Works stated last year when $25,000 was voted that it was in the public interest to build a dock there, but now the government comes forward and says that the Minister of Public Works did not know what he was talking about last year. When this money was voted they paid that company $34,000 and appointed them their agents contrary to the law which says:	that no public money can
be expended over $5,000 unless let by tender, except it is a work of necessity or where in the opinion of that department it can be better done by the officers of the department. Wliat employees of the government are doing this work ? It is done by an American Arm with its office in New York, who have a gang of men building a railway and they are dumping the ballast down the side of a hill and get $1.25 a yard for the filling. And what is the dock for ? Some one said yesterday that a large village was going up in the neighbourhood. Why it is seven miles across. This gentleman says that there is not a man living within seven miles of it, nor a man who will use it except this American pulp company. The Minister of Justice says that the Clarkes, of Toronto, are British subjects,, but they are in New York and have been there for years doing business' with their associates.
I understand the Minister of Justice said that the firm of Mossom, Boyd and Company, of Bobcaygeon, are engaged with this firm.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. I said they were the owners of the adjoining limits ; that they intend putting up a large pulp mill in the neighbourhood on a power they have in the immediate vicinity ; that this will enable them to export the pulp, and that it is necessary for them to have wharf facilities in this place. That I know from one of the Mr. Boyd's, who told me so himself a year and a half ago or so,

in Quebec, and from the gentleman who acted as his lawyer-I forget his name but lie is a well-lmown lawyer in Toronto.
